questions.q: Which mosquito genus lays its eggs in floating rafts?
questions.expl: Culex eggs are laid vertically side by side, forming a characteristic floating raft on the water surface.

questions.q: Sperm received during mating is stored by the female mosquito in organs called:
questions.expl: Female mosquitoes store sperm in specialised organs called spermathecae for later fertilisation of eggs.

questions.q: The classical malaria symptom sequence of cold, hot, and sweating stages (paroxysms) corresponds to which biological event?
options: Synchronous rupture of infected red blood cells
questions.expl: Paroxysms — the classic cold, hot, and sweating stage sequence — correspond to the synchronous rupture of infected red blood cells (schizogony) during the blood stage of the parasite's life cycle.

questions.q: What shape are the compound eyes of a mosquito?
questions.expl: Mosquito compound eyes are kidney-shaped and made up of many light detectors called ommatidia.

questions.q: Which mode of reproduction, exemplified by the tsetse fly (Glossina spp.), involves eggs hatching within the female with larvae nourished internally and born directly?
questions.expl: Viviparous reproduction in tsetse flies is critical for understanding African trypanosomiasis epidemiology, as larvae are nourished internally and born directly.

questions.q: Yersinia pestis, the causative agent of plague, is categorized in the lecture under which group of vector-borne pathogens?
questions.expl: Yersinia pestis is a bacterium, listed alongside Borrelia and Rickettsia species as vector-borne bacteria.

questions.q: How long does it take for bed bug eggs to hatch?
questions.expl: Bed bug eggs hatch after 8-11 days.

questions.q: Exopterygota undergo which type of metamorphosis?
questions.expl: Exopterygota undergo gradual (incomplete) metamorphosis, termed hemimetabolism.

questions.q: How long do mosquitoes typically take to develop from egg to adult?
questions.expl: Mosquitoes typically develop from egg to adult in about 7-14 days, depending on temperature and species.

questions.q: The arachnid body is divided into which two main regions?
questions.expl: Arachnids have a two-part body: the prosoma (cephalothorax) and opisthosoma (abdomen).

questions.q: Millipedes belong to which arthropod class?
questions.expl: Millipedes are classified under Diplopoda, distinct from centipedes (Chilopoda).

questions.q: What is the critical vector responsible for amplifying yellow fever into large urban epidemics?
questions.expl: The urban cycle of yellow fever is driven by the highly domesticated, container-breeding Aedes aegypti, which bites a viremic human and can then transmit the virus widely among dense urban populations.

questions.q: The insect body is divided into how many main regions?
questions.expl: Insects have a three-part body plan: head, thorax, and abdomen.

questions.q: A mosquito's longevity has little bearing on its ability to transmit malaria, since the parasite develops almost instantly inside the vector.
questions.expl: Longevity matters greatly: the parasite requires time to complete its extrinsic incubation period inside the mosquito. A long adult lifespan is essential for the mosquito to survive long enough to become infectious and transmit the parasite.

questions.q: What is the correct sequence of mosquito development?
questions.expl: The correct sequence is Egg, Larva, Pupa, Adult — mosquitoes undergo complete metamorphosis (holometabolism).

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a symptom/effect associated with bed bug bites?
questions.expl: Bed bug bites are associated with distress, anaemia, nervousness, insomnia, nausea, vomiting, chills, and iron deficiency in children - not joint deformity.

questions.q: Culex quinquefasciatus is a good vector for transmitting:
questions.expl: Culex quinquefasciatus is the primary vector of Wuchereria bancrofti, the cause of most lymphatic filariasis cases.

questions.q: Mosquito larvae are primarily:
questions.expl: Mosquito larvae are entirely aquatic, legless, and filter-feed on organic matter at or near the water surface.

questions.q: Approximately how long can adult bed bugs live?
questions.expl: Adult bed bugs can live for relatively long periods, approximately 1-4 years.

questions.q: Target-site resistance of Anopheles to pyrethroids is caused by mutation of the:
questions.expl: Pyrethroid target-site resistance arises from knockdown resistance (kdr) mutations in the voltage-gated sodium channel, the pyrethroid's target site. Cytochrome P450 and acetylcholinesterase changes relate to metabolic resistance instead.

questions.q: Which mosquito species forms the critical epidemiological bridge in the rural (intermediate) cycle of yellow fever, between viremic monkeys and humans?
questions.expl: Aedes simpsoni, a semi-domestic species breeding in both tree holes and domestic containers, feeds on viremic monkeys that descend to forage near farms, then bites humans — bridging the forest reservoir and rural communities.

questions.q: In holometabolous insects such as mosquitoes, the larval stage typically occupies the same habitat as the adult.
questions.expl: Holometabolous larvae and adults often occupy entirely different habitats — mosquito larvae are aquatic while adults are aerial — requiring separate control strategies.

questions.q: The exoskeleton of an insect is made up of:
questions.expl: An insect's tough outer cuticle (exoskeleton) is composed of chitin, not collagen, cellulose, or keratin.

questions.q: Which region of the insect gut is the primary site of digestion and absorption, lined by the peritrophic membrane?
questions.expl: The midgut is the primary digestion and absorption site, lined by the protective peritrophic membrane.

questions.q: Anopheles larvae, unlike culicine larvae, lack a:
questions.expl: Anopheles larvae lack a respiratory siphon entirely; they breathe via paired spiracles and lie horizontally at the water surface, unlike culicine larvae which hang at an angle using a siphon.

questions.q: St. Louis Encephalitis and Japanese Encephalitis are both caused by viruses of which genus, and are primarily transmitted by which mosquito genus?
questions.expl: Both St. Louis Encephalitis and Japanese Encephalitis are caused by Flaviviruses and are primarily transmitted by Culex mosquitoes, with wild birds (and pigs, for JE) serving as amplifying reservoir hosts.

questions.q: How many larval instars does an Anopheles larva pass through before pupation?
questions.expl: Anopheles larvae pass through 4 instars, completing development in about 7 days in tropical conditions (up to 14 days in temperate regions).

questions.q: Which genus lays eggs in sticky, compact rosette-shaped masses attached to the undersides of aquatic plant leaves?
questions.expl: Mansonia eggs are laid in sticky compact masses arranged in rosettes, attached to the undersides of aquatic plant leaves — a unique strategy linked to its plant-dependent larval stage.

questions.q: The Duffy antigen in humans affects susceptibility to which disease?
questions.expl: Plasmodium vivax requires the Duffy antigen receptor to invade red blood cells; Duffy-negative individuals (common in Africa) are largely resistant to P. vivax malaria.

questions.q: Which mosquito genus is primarily responsible for filariasis transmission in urban, insanitary water in Ghana?
questions.expl: Culex quinquefasciatus, breeding in polluted stagnant urban water (drains, ditches), is the primary vector of lymphatic filariasis in urban settings.

questions.q: How many sections (segments) make up the mosquito abdomen?
questions.expl: The abdomen has 10 sections/segments.

questions.q: WHOPES-recommended insecticides for mosquito control include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.expl: WHOPES recommends four classes: organochlorines, organophosphates, carbamates, and pyrethroids. Glyphosate is a herbicide, not an insecticide class.

questions.q: Which arthropod group is responsible for transmitting the greatest proportion of arboviruses globally?
questions.expl: Mosquitoes transmit approximately 72% of arboviruses globally, making them by far the most important arthropod vector group for these viruses, followed distantly by ixodid ticks at around 18%.

questions.q: Haemolymph in insects can exert hydraulic pressure that assists processes like wing expansion after moulting.
questions.expl: Haemolymph's mechanical role includes exerting hydraulic pressure that assists wing expansion, appendage extension, and eclosion from the pupal case.

questions.q: The key difference between crustaceans and insects is that crustaceans:
questions.expl: Unlike insects, which excrete via Malpighian tubules, crustaceans excrete nitrogenous waste through the green gland (antennal gland).

questions.q: Infestation of the eyelashes by the pubic louse is termed:
questions.expl: When the pubic louse infests the eyelashes, the condition is called pediculosis ciliaris.

questions.q: Body lice are described as 'gregarious', meaning they are typically found:
options: Clustered together, e.g. in clothing seams
questions.expl: Body lice are gregarious, commonly found clustered together in the seams of clothing.

questions.q: Louse eggs are laid loosely and can easily fall off the hair or clothing.
questions.expl: Louse eggs are firmly cemented/glued into place on hair shafts or clothing fibres, which is why they are hard to remove.

questions.q: Endophagic mosquitoes prefer to:
questions.expl: Endophagic describes a mosquito that feeds indoors (en- = in, -phagic = feeding).

questions.q: The terminal fine tubes of the tracheal system that end directly in cells for gas exchange are called:
questions.expl: Tracheoles are the finest terminal branches of the tracheal system, delivering oxygen directly to individual cells.

questions.q: Which secondary bacterial skin infection is mentioned as a complication of body louse infestation?
questions.expl: Secondary bacterial infections such as impetigo may complicate body louse infestation.

questions.q: What shape is the bed bug's abdomen often compared to?
questions.expl: The bed bug's abdomen is described as lemon shaped.

questions.q: Why are some Anopheles species more efficient malaria vectors than others?
options: Differences in feeding behaviour and host preference
Only female Anopheles exist in some populations
questions.expl: Vector efficiency depends heavily on behavioural traits — anthropophilic feeding preference, endophagic/endophilic habits, and host contact patterns — which vary between Anopheles species.

questions.q: What disease is transmitted by the Mansonia mosquito?
questions.expl: Mansonia africana and M. uniformis are key vectors of Wuchereria bancrofti, the cause of lymphatic filariasis.

questions.q: The halteres are a true second pair of flight wings used to generate lift.
questions.expl: Halteres are modified hind wings used for balance and steering, not for generating lift; only the front pair of wings is used for flying.

questions.q: Compared with the body and head louse, the pubic louse is:
questions.expl: The pubic louse is smaller than the other two types of lice.

questions.q: Larval source reduction, as a mosquito control method, refers to:
options: Eliminating stagnant water and breeding sites
Spraying insecticide on adult resting sites
questions.expl: Source reduction means eliminating or modifying breeding sites (e.g. removing stagnant water), distinct from chemical control (spraying) or genetic control (sterile males).

questions.q: Roughly how many nits per day does a female head louse cement to hair, according to the epidemiology section?
questions.expl: In the epidemiology section, the female head louse is described as living 1 month and laying 7-10 nits per day.

questions.q: What is the primary mode of transmission for the pubic louse?
questions.expl: Pubic louse infestation occurs primarily through sexual contact.

questions.q: What type of atmosphere does the pubic louse prefer?
questions.expl: The pubic louse prefers a humid atmosphere.

questions.q: What is required for each bed bug nymphal instar to progress to the next stage?
questions.expl: Each nymphal instar requires at least one blood meal before it can moult to the next stage.

questions.q: The Malpighian tubule in insects is analogous to which organ in humans?
questions.expl: Malpighian tubules regulate the osmotic and nitrogenous waste balance of the haemolymph, functionally analogous to the human kidney.

questions.q: Mosquitoes belong to which insect order?
questions.expl: Mosquitoes belong to Order Diptera ('true flies'), Family Culicidae.

questions.q: What structure in mosquitoes is critical for detecting CO2 from a host?
questions.expl: The maxillary palps carry the primary CO2-sensing receptors that help mosquitoes locate a host.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a function of insect haemolymph?
options: Carrying excretory products to excretory organs
questions.expl: Insects lack haemoglobin; oxygen delivery occurs via the tracheal system through diffusion, not via haemolymph.

questions.q: The pupal stage of the Anopheles mosquito is non-feeding but remains highly mobile in water.
questions.expl: True — the pupa does not feed, but it is highly mobile and retreats quickly from disturbance using its paddles.

questions.q: What characteristic odour is associated with a heavy bed bug infestation?
questions.expl: A heavy bed bug infestation may produce a sickly sweet smell, likened to rotting raspberries.

questions.q: Hatching of the insect egg, marking the start of larval/nymphal life, is termed:
questions.expl: Eclosion marks hatching from the egg, the beginning of the immature developmental stages.

questions.q: Which mosquito species is the primary vector of Wuchereria bancrofti in urban settings?
questions.expl: Culex quinquefasciatus, which breeds prolifically in insanitary, stagnant, polluted water such as drains and open sewers, is the primary urban vector of Wuchereria bancrofti, the cause of most lymphatic filariasis.

questions.q: Which of the following arthropods has muscle-powered wings for locomotion?
questions.expl: Among these options, only the mosquito (an insect) possesses wings; spiders, scorpions, and crabs do not fly.

questions.q: What is the most diagnostic visual feature of the genus Aedes, especially Ae. aegypti?
options: Plain brown coloration with no markings
Black-and-white silvery scale banding, including a lyre-shaped thoracic pattern
A single red stripe down the abdomen
questions.expl: Aedes adults display a striking black-and-white silvery scale pattern, including banded ('ringed') legs and, in Ae. aegypti, a distinctive lyre-shaped white marking on the dorsal thorax.

questions.q: In the five-stage IVM process, what is the purpose of Stage 1 (Situation Analysis & Survey)?
options: To establish a baseline assessment defining the problem and evidence base
To distribute insecticide-treated nets to households
To train community health workers exclusively
questions.expl: Stage 1, Situation Analysis & Survey, establishes a rigorous baseline assessment — identifying vector species, local ecology, resistance status, and socioeconomic context — that provides the evidence base for all subsequent program decisions.

questions.q: Which sexual distinction is true of male culicine mosquitoes compared to females?
options: Males have short palps and pilose antennae
Males have long palps and plumose antennae
questions.expl: Male culicines have long palps and plumose (bushy) antennae used to detect female pheromones, whereas females have short palps, pilose antennae, and abdominal scales (a feature absent in Anopheles of either sex).

questions.q: Approximately how many eggs does a female head louse lay per day?
questions.expl: The female head louse lays about 6-8 eggs per day.

questions.q: A female Anopheles mosquito bites man because:
options: She needs a blood meal for egg development
She is attracted to movement only
questions.expl: Female mosquitoes need the protein from a blood meal to mature their eggs; this is why only females bite.

questions.q: Bed bugs belong to which insect Order?
questions.expl: Bed bugs belong to the Order Hemiptera (the 'true bugs').

questions.q: Complete metamorphosis (holometabolism) is advantageous mainly because:
options: Larvae and adults occupy different niches, avoiding resource competition
Males are eliminated from the population
questions.expl: Because larvae and adults look and behave completely differently (e.g. aquatic larvae vs. aerial adult mosquitoes), they exploit different habitats and resources, avoiding competition with each other.

questions.q: How many ventral maxillae stylets does the louse possess?
questions.expl: The louse has 2 ventral maxillae stylets, which work alongside the mandible and hypopharynx.

questions.q: Where do the rudimentary, non-functional wings of the bed bug lie?
options: They are entirely absent, with no trace
questions.expl: The rudimentary, non-functional wings (hemielytra) of the bed bug lie over the meso- and metathorax.

questions.q: Why are standard surface-applied larvicides generally ineffective against Mansonia larvae?
options: Mansonia larvae are resistant to all chemical compounds
Mansonia larvae obtain oxygen from plant tissue rather than the water surface
Mansonia larvae live exclusively on dry land
Mansonia larvae are too large to be affected by larvicides
questions.expl: Because Mansonia larvae pierce aquatic plant tissue (such as water lettuce) for oxygen rather than surfacing, oil-based surface larvicides cannot reach them — control instead requires removing or treating the aquatic vegetation itself.

questions.q: An Anopheles mosquito's resting posture is characteristically at:
questions.expl: Adult Anopheles rest at a sharp upward angle (45° or greater) to the surface — a key diagnostic field feature, distinguishing them from culicines, which rest parallel to the surface.

questions.q: Which population group is most commonly affected by head lice?
questions.expl: Children are most commonly affected by head lice infestation.

questions.q: What sensory structure is used by mosquitoes to sense changes in wind current?
questions.expl: Mosquito antennae detect CO2, body heat, and air currents.

questions.q: Culex pipiens fatigans, known as the 'rain barrel' or house mosquito, is the primary vector for which disease?
questions.expl: Culex pipiens fatigans, the 'rain barrel' or house mosquito, is the primary vector of lymphatic filariasis and breeds strongly in insanitary, polluted water such as drains and ditches.

questions.q: The primary goal of the insect excretory system, achieved mainly via the Malpighian tubules, is to:
options: Maintain a constant internal environment by regulating pH and osmotic concentration
questions.expl: The excretory system maintains homeostasis by regulating the pH and osmotic concentration of the haemolymph.

questions.q: How are louse nits typically described in shape and colour?
questions.expl: Louse nits are oval and white, and possess a small lid called an operculum.

questions.q: In Endopterygota, wings develop:
questions.expl: Endopterygote insects develop wings internally during the larval stage, emerging fully formed in the adult.

questions.q: What is the primary reason only female mosquitoes bite humans?
questions.expl: True — only female mosquitoes require a blood meal (for egg protein); males feed on nectar and plant sugars.

questions.q: Which needle-like mouthpart structures penetrate the skin to reach blood vessels?
questions.expl: The maxillae are needle-like structures that penetrate the skin to reach blood vessels.

questions.q: Which parasite listed in the lecture is the causative agent of African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness)?
questions.expl: Trypanosoma brucei causes African trypanosomiasis, while T. cruzi causes Chagas disease in the Americas.

questions.q: How many larval instars (developmental stages) does a mosquito larva pass through?
questions.expl: Mosquito larvae pass through four larval instars.

questions.q: How many segments make up the body louse's antennae?
questions.expl: The body louse has short, 5-segmented antennae.

questions.q: Organophosphate insecticides generally have a longer residual activity (6–12 months) than pyrethroids.
questions.expl: Organophosphates actually have a shorter residual activity of only 2–3 months, are biodegradable, and have low mammalian toxicity — unlike DDT-type organochlorines, which can persist for 6–12 months.

questions.q: Aedes aegypti is a primary vector of which disease(s)?
questions.expl: Aedes aegypti is the primary vector of dengue, yellow fever, Zika, and chikungunya.

questions.q: In most non-blood-feeding insects, saliva primarily moistens the mouthparts and contains digestive enzymes such as amylase.
questions.expl: Saliva normally moistens mouthparts and aids digestion (e.g., amylase in cockroaches); medically significant components like anticoagulins are most prominent in blood-feeding insects.

questions.q: Which of these is given as an example of a 'natural' mosquito breeding habitat?
questions.expl: Natural habitats mentioned include tree holes and bamboo stumps.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a factor that attracts body lice to a host?
questions.expl: Body lice are attracted by odour, sweat chemistry, body temperature, humidity, and darkness (e.g. beneath clothing) - not bright light.

questions.q: Halteres in mosquitoes function as:
questions.expl: Halteres are modified hindwings that act as a gyroscopic organ, enabling balance and precise in-flight manoeuvring.

questions.q: Organophosphate insecticides are characterised by which of the following?
options: Very effective but with short residual activity of 2-3 months
High mammalian toxicity used only outdoors
questions.expl: Organophosphates are very effective insecticides but have a short residual activity of about 2-3 months and are relatively expensive to produce.

questions.q: The shed exoskeleton left behind after moulting is referred to as the:
questions.expl: The cast-off skin from moulting is called the exuviae.

questions.q: The insect alimentary canal is divided into how many main regions?
questions.expl: The alimentary canal comprises three regions: foregut, midgut, and hindgut.

questions.q: Controlling mosquito populations by releasing sterile males to disrupt mating is known as:
questions.expl: Sterile Insect Technique (SIT) suppresses populations by releasing sterile males that mate with wild females without producing viable offspring.

questions.q: The gonotrophic cycle refers to:
options: Blood feeding, egg maturation, and oviposition
questions.expl: The gonotrophic cycle is the repeated cycle of blood feeding, egg maturation, and oviposition in female mosquitoes.

questions.q: Which insect sensory receptors are primarily responsible for taste and smell?
questions.expl: Chemoreceptors, located on antennae and palps, are responsible for taste and smell.

questions.q: Why do Anopheles larvae lie parallel to the water surface?
options: To breathe via spiracles, since they lack a respiratory siphon
questions.expl: Anopheles larvae lack a siphon entirely, so they lie horizontally at the surface to access air through paired spiracles on abdominal segment 8.

questions.q: Where does itching occur in pubic louse infestation?
options: Only in infested areas of the body
questions.expl: Itching from pubic lice occurs only in the areas of the body that are infested.

questions.q: How long does the general louse egg stage last before hatching?
questions.expl: The general louse egg stage lasts 6-10 days before hatching.

questions.q: Harmonic convergence in mosquito mating refers to:
options: Synchronisation of male and female wingbeat frequency
questions.expl: Harmonic convergence is courtship behaviour where a male mosquito modulates his wingbeat frequency to match the female's.

questions.q: Bed bugs are described as 'gregarious', meaning they tend to:
questions.expl: Bed bugs are gregarious in nature, often found aggregated together in harbourages.

questions.q: Which structures in the hindgut reabsorb up to 90% of water from the forming faecal pellet?
questions.expl: Rectal papillae in the rectum reabsorb up to 90% of water, a key adaptation for water conservation.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best describe the difference between insects and arachnids?

options.note: Arachnids have a fused cephalothorax; insects have separate head, thorax and abdomen.
Shared arthropod trait — not a distinguishing feature between the two groups.

options.text: The presence of four pairs of walking legs
options.note: Classic distinguishing feature — arachnids have 4 leg pairs (8 legs), insects have 3 (6 legs).

options.text: The presence of a waxy cuticle
options.note: Both groups have a cuticle — shared arthropod trait, not a difference.
Insects have antennae; arachnids lack antennae entirely.

questions.stem: In insects:

options.text: The exoskeleton is rigid and prevents increase in size
options.note: This is exactly why insects must moult (ecdysis) periodically to grow.

options.text: A gradual metamorphosis is known as holometabolous
options.note: Gradual metamorphosis is hemimetabolous. Holometabolous = complete metamorphosis with a pupal stage.

options.text: A proboscis is only found in haematophagous insects
options.note: Many non-blood-feeding insects (e.g. butterflies) also have a proboscis.

options.text: The function of the spermatheca is to produce a large number of spermatozoa
options.note: The spermatheca stores sperm — it does not produce it.

options.text: The crop serves as a temporary food store
options.note: Correct — the crop is a temporary storage organ in the insect foregut.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best describe insects:

options.note: Most insects are oviparous (egg-laying); ovoviviparity is the exception, not the rule.

options.text: The malpighian tubules extract urine and other metabolic waste from the haemolymph
options.note: Correct — Malpighian tubules are the main insect excretory organ.

options.text: The main function of the haemolymph is to provide mechanical pressure
options.note: Haemolymph's main roles are nutrient/waste transport and immune defence; hydrostatic pressure is a secondary function.

options.text: The male genitalia is of taxonomic importance
options.note: True — genitalia morphology is commonly used to distinguish closely related species.

options.text: Growth is restricted to the immature stages of their life cycle
options.note: Correct — most adult insects have a hardened cuticle and no longer moult or grow.

questions.stem: Vector control methods suitable for community involvement should:

options.note: A community method must actually work.
Cost must be manageable for the community.

options.text: be acceptable and compatible with local customs
options.note: Cultural acceptability drives uptake and sustainability.
Community members need to grasp and apply the method themselves.

options.text: should involve vector control specialists and modern equipment
options.note: This contradicts the premise of community-level involvement, which favours simple, accessible methods.

questions.stem: The most reliable way to distinguish between adult Anopheles and Culicine mosquitoes is to examine:

options.note: Antennae differ mainly by sex (plumose vs pilose), not reliably by genus.
Not the standard reliable distinguishing feature.
Classic answer — Anopheles females have palps as long as the proboscis; Culicines have short palps.
Culicines have abdominal scales and Anopheles typically lack them, but palps remain the more reliable/definitive feature taught.

questions.stem: During the gonotrophic cycle in Mosquitoes:

options.text: the blood fed female seeks a suitable habitat to lay her eggs
options.note: Correct — oviposition site-seeking is part of the cycle.

options.text: two blood meals are needed for the eggs to mature
options.note: Typically only ONE blood meal is needed per gonotrophic cycle.

options.text: the speed of digestion of the blood meal depends on temperature
options.note: Correct — blood meal digestion is a temperature-dependent metabolic process.

options.text: sperms are stored in the spermatheca
options.note: Correct — females store sperm from a single mating for life.

options.text: the eggs that are laid are able to withstand long periods of desiccation
options.note: True for Aedes, but not for most Culex/Anopheles eggs, which are the general case here.

questions.stem: In mosquitoes:

options.text: the most distinguishing feature is their rigid forwardly projecting proboscis
options.note: Correct — the classic mosquito identification feature.

options.text: they can be sexed by examination of their antennae
options.note: Correct — males have plumose (bushy) antennae, females have pilose (sparse) antennae.

options.text: Oxygen for larval respiration is aerial
options.note: Correct — larvae breathe atmospheric air at the water surface via siphon/spiracles.

options.text: all anopheline larvae possess a siphon
options.note: Anopheline larvae LACK a siphon — this is a Culicine trait; Anophelines lie parallel to the surface instead.

options.text: the pupae can be sexed by examining the tip of the abdomen
options.note: Correct — genital lobes visible at the abdomen tip differ by sex.

questions.stem: Effective mosquito control methods include

options.note: Reduces breeding sites.
Alters habitat to prevent breeding.
Controls water levels to disrupt larval habitats.
SIT is a genuine vector control method.
IRS is a standard, well-established control method.

questions.stem: Aedes mosquitoes involved in the transmission of yellow fever virus in Africa involve:

options.note: Vector of the rural/intermediate yellow fever cycle (monkey-to-human bridge).
Not a recognised major yellow fever vector.
Vector of the sylvatic (monkey-to-monkey) cycle.
Not a primary yellow fever vector.
Vector of the urban (human-to-human) cycle.

questions.stem: The disease pathogens and parasites that houseflies can transmit due to their dirty habits include:

options.note: Mechanically transmitted via contaminated fly parts.
Mechanical transmission of eggs is documented.
Documented mechanical vector for the virus.
Classic housefly-transmitted enteric pathogen.
Transmitted by the tsetse fly, not the housefly.

questions.stem: The most appropriate methods to control Houseflies include

options.note: Fly barriers are more associated with tsetse control, not standard housefly control.
The primary housefly control method — removing breeding material (waste/faeces).
A valid, standard housefly control method.
Impoundment is a mosquito larval control method — houseflies breed in organic waste, not water bodies.
Not a recognised housefly control method.

questions.stem: Even though the Onchocerciasis Control Programme has been heralded as a very successful project the major problems encountered include:

options.text: the ability of the Blackflies to fly long distances
options.note: Reinvasion via long-range blackfly dispersal was a genuine documented challenge.

options.text: Non compliance of treatment regimen by local inhabitants
options.note: A genuine documented challenge to the programme.

options.text: resistance of adults to the appropriate organochlorines and organophosphates
options.note: Insecticide resistance was a documented OCP challenge.

options.text: inability to locate breeding sites of larvae
options.note: Breeding sites (fast-flowing rivers) were well mapped and targeted for larviciding — not the challenge.
Sustained funding was a recurring challenge for the long-running programme.

questions.stem: Which of the following flies are known to cause myiasis: cutaneous obligatory traumatic

options.note: Classified among myiasis-associated flies in standard teaching.
Cochliomyia hominivorax — classic obligate traumatic myiasis agent.
Chrysomya bezziana — classic obligate traumatic myiasis agent.
Cordylobia anthropophaga — causes cutaneous myiasis.
Too general a term — not a specific myiasis-causing group.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best describe the life cycle of blackflies:

options.text: eggs are always laid in swift flowing water
options.note: Correct — Simulium breeds in fast-flowing streams/rapids.

options.text: mature larvae remains sedentary for long periods of time
options.note: Larvae are active filter-feeders while attached, not dormant.

options.text: prominent respiratory filaments are found on mature larvae
options.note: Prominent respiratory gills are a pupal feature, not larval.

options.text: empty pupal cases are of taxonomic importance
options.note: Correct — pupal case morphology is used for species identification.

options.text: Simulium flies deposit eggs in favourite communal oviposition sites
options.note: Correct — blackflies show gregarious/communal oviposition behaviour.

questions.stem: The characteristic forwardly projecting proboscis of a mosquito comprises of the following parts:

options.note: Forms the sheath of the proboscis.
Part of the piercing stylet bundle.
This is a tarsal (leg) structure, not part of the mouthparts.
Part of the thorax, not the mouthparts.
Part of the proboscis — carries the salivary duct.

questions.stem: In Malaria Control Programmes the problems associated with conventional insecticidal spraying include

options.text: objection by residents in the home
options.note: Documented issue — residents refusing indoor spraying.
A genuine logistical and financial challenge.
Documented — mosquitoes developing exophilic/avoidance behaviour after IRS.

A single red stripe down the abdomen

questions.stem: Which sexual distinction is true of male culicine mosquitoes compared to females?

options.text: Males have short palps and pilose antennae
Males have long palps and plumose (bushy) antennae

questions.explanation: Male culicines have long palps and plumose (bushy) antennae used to detect female pheromones, whereas females have short palps, pilose antennae, and abdominal scales (a feature absent in Anopheles of either sex).

questions.stem: Which control approach involves applying insecticide to interior walls and surfaces where mosquitoes rest after feeding?
questions.explanation: Indoor Residual Spraying (IRS) applies insecticide to interior walls and resting surfaces, killing mosquitoes after they feed and rest indoors. It is highly effective against endophilic species like many Anopheles, but less useful against exophilic species like Aedes.

The main function of the haemolymph is to provide mechanical pressure

questions.stem: DEET (N,N-Diethyl-meta-toluamide) is best described as which type of vector control tool?

options.text: A larvicide applied to water bodies
A topical repellent that deters but does not kill mosquitoes

questions.explanation: DEET is the gold-standard repellent, providing the longest-lasting, broad-spectrum personal protection. Repellents create a chemical barrier that deters biting rather than killing the insect, and require frequent reapplication.

questions.stem: External openings through which air enters the insect tracheal system are called:
questions.explanation: Spiracles are the external openings located on the meso- and metathoraces and abdominal segments.

questions.stem: In the family Muscidae, the flies of greatest medical importance include

Musca domestica also known as the latrine fly
Fannia canicularis, the lesser house fly

questions.explanation: Correct species and common name.

questions.explanation: The body louse has short, 5-segmented antennae.

questions.explanation: Small size is listed as one of the traits underlying insects' ecological dominance, alongside short life cycle, flight, and reproductive capacity.

questions.explanation: Class Insecta is the largest arthropod class and includes the medically important insects named.

The terminal abdominal segment is bilobed

questions.stem: What is the chronic clinical hallmark of long-standing lymphatic filariasis, caused by blocked lymph flow?
questions.explanation: Adult filarial worms residing in lymphatic vessels block lymph flow, causing progressive lymphedema that, in severe long-standing cases, produces the grossly enlarged, hyperkeratotic limbs characteristic of elephantiasis.

questions.stem: What is the most diagnostic visual feature of the genus Aedes, especially Ae. aegypti?

Black-and-white silvery scale banding, including a lyre-shaped thoracic pattern
A single red stripe down the abdomen

questions.explanation: Aedes adults display a striking black-and-white silvery scale pattern, including banded ('ringed') legs and, in Ae. aegypti, a distinctive lyre-shaped white marking on the dorsal thorax.

questions.stem: Which culicine genus lays eggs singly on damp substrate and is resistant to desiccation via diapause?
questions.explanation: Aedes eggs are laid singly on damp substrate at the waterline or in small containers and are highly resistant to desiccation through diapause, allowing them to remain viable for months without water.

questions.stem: Aedes aegypti is primarily a nocturnal, indoor-resting mosquito, similar to Anopheles funestus.
questions.explanation: Aedes aegypti is a vicious day-time biter, with peak activity at dawn and dusk, and is strongly exophilic and exophagic — feeding and resting outdoors — unlike the nocturnal, endophilic Anopheles funestus.

questions.stem: The Onchocerciasis Control Programme was carried out for over 15 years because

options.text: The rivers in which the black fly breed were too long and inaccessible
There was a problem of insecticidal resistance
The parasite lives in the vector for a very long time
The West African countries involved could not raise enough funds

questions.stem: Which transmission pattern describes malaria that is present at high, constant intensity throughout the year?
questions.explanation: Holoendemic transmission refers to year-round malaria transmission at very high, constant intensity, as opposed to hyperendemic (constantly high incidence), mesoendemic (seasonal), or hypoendemic (low incidence, epidemic-prone) patterns.

questions.stem: Dengue fever is colloquially known as 'breakbone fever' because of which clinical feature?
questions.explanation: Dengue's nickname 'breakbone fever' reflects the severe joint and bone pain that characterizes the classic illness, which is primarily transmitted by Aedes aegypti and increasingly Ae. albopictus.

questions.explanation: Both St. Louis Encephalitis and Japanese Encephalitis are caused by Flaviviruses and are primarily transmitted by Culex mosquitoes, with wild birds (and pigs, for JE) serving as amplifying reservoir hosts.

questions.stem: Like the body louse, the bed bug's body is flattened in which orientation?
questions.explanation: Bed bugs are flattened dorsoventrally, similar to the body louse, allowing them to hide in narrow cracks.

questions.stem: Culex decens is described as an important disease vector in Ghana.
questions.explanation: Culex decens is described as abundant but not implicated in disease transmission in Ghana.

questions.explanation: Correct — established gregarious egg-laying behaviour.

questions.stem: Which mosquito species forms the critical epidemiological bridge in the rural (intermediate) cycle of yellow fever, between viremic monkeys and humans?
questions.explanation: Aedes simpsoni, a semi-domestic species breeding in both tree holes and domestic containers, feeds on viremic monkeys that descend to forage near farms, then bites humans — bridging the forest reservoir and rural communities.

questions.stem: Which of these is listed as an additional bed bug control measure besides structure proofing and chemical control?
questions.explanation: Impregnated bed nets are listed as another control method against bed bugs.

questions.stem: Draining or modifying breeding sites to prevent mosquito development is an example of:
questions.explanation: Habitat change/source reduction is classified as physical control.

questions.q: The scientific study of micro-organisms too small to be seen with the naked eye is called:
questions.expl: Microbiology is the scientific study of micro-organisms — bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa, and algae — invisible to the naked eye.

questions.q: Which discipline is defined as the study of microorganisms that cause human disease, including pathogenesis and host immune response?
questions.expl: Medical Microbiology focuses on disease-causing microorganisms, the nature of infection, host immune response, and treatment principles.

questions.q: Which applied discipline integrates laboratory science with clinical care, identifying pathogens from patient specimens to guide therapy?
questions.expl: Clinical Microbiology applies lab science to patient care, identifying pathogens and guiding therapeutic decisions.

questions.q: The study of eukaryotic parasites such as protozoa and helminths and their impact on human health is called:
questions.expl: Parasitology covers eukaryotic parasites, including protozoa and helminths.

questions.q: The Malpighian tubule in insects is analogous to which organ in humans?
questions.expl: Entomology, in the medical context, studies insects and arthropods of medical significance, particularly disease vectors.

questions.q: Entomology is merely a zoological curiosity with little real relevance to clinical microbiology.
questions.expl: The lecture stresses that entomology is a critical pillar of medical and clinical microbiology, since most devastating infectious diseases worldwide are vector-borne.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed among the vector-borne viruses discussed in the lecture?
questions.expl: Hepatitis B is bloodborne/sexually transmitted, not among the arthropod-vectored viruses listed (which include Dengue, Zika, and West Nile).

questions.q: Yersinia pestis, the causative agent of plague, is categorized in the lecture under which group of vector-borne pathogens?
questions.expl: Yersinia pestis is a bacterium, listed alongside Borrelia and Rickettsia species as vector-borne bacteria.

questions.q: Which parasite listed in the lecture is the causative agent of African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness)?
questions.expl: Trypanosoma brucei causes African trypanosomiasis, while T. cruzi causes Chagas disease in the Americas.

questions.q: Wuchereria bancrofti and Brugia malayi/timori, listed among vector-borne parasites, are associated with which condition?
questions.expl: Wuchereria bancrofti and Brugia species are filarial worms that cause lymphatic filariasis.

questions.q: Onchocerca volvulus, a parasite listed in the lecture, is the cause of:
questions.expl: Onchocerca volvulus causes onchocerciasis, commonly known as river blindness.

questions.q: All arthropods share a common body plan featuring a protective exoskeleton called the cuticle and jointed appendages.
questions.expl: Arthropods share a tough outer cuticle (exoskeleton) and jointed appendages such as legs and antennae as defining features.

questions.q: Approximately what percentage of all known animal species do arthropods comprise?
questions.expl: Arthropods make up roughly 85% of all known animal species, with over 1 million described species.

questions.q: Which class of Phylum Arthropoda is the largest and includes houseflies, mosquitoes, lice, and beetles?
questions.expl: Class Insecta is the largest arthropod class and includes the medically important insects named.

questions.q: Millipedes belong to which arthropod class?
questions.expl: These organisms belong to Class Arachnida, an important group of disease vectors.

questions.q: Which arthropod group is responsible for transmitting the greatest proportion of arboviruses globally?
questions.expl: Millipedes are classified under Diplopoda, distinct from centipedes (Chilopoda).

questions.q: How many pairs of legs do insects (Class Insecta) typically have?
questions.expl: Insects have 3 pairs of legs (6 legs total), one of the defining features of the class.

questions.q: How many pairs of legs do arachnids (Class Arachnida) typically have?
questions.expl: Arachnids have 4 pairs of legs (8 legs total), distinguishing them from insects.

questions.q: The insect body is divided into how many main regions?
questions.expl: Insects have a three-part body plan: head, thorax, and abdomen.

questions.q: The arachnid body is divided into which two main regions?
questions.expl: Arachnids have a two-part body: the prosoma (cephalothorax) and opisthosoma (abdomen).

questions.q: The key difference between crustaceans and insects is that crustaceans:
questions.expl: Insects respire via a tracheal system that delivers air directly to tissues.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a trait contributing to insects' extraordinary evolutionary success?
questions.expl: Small (not large) body size is listed as advantageous, minimizing food and shelter requirements for survival in marginal environments.

questions.q: Small body size in insects helps minimize food and shelter requirements, enabling survival in marginal environments.
questions.expl: Small size is listed as one of the traits underlying insects' ecological dominance, alongside short life cycle, flight, and reproductive capacity.

questions.q: Mosquitoes belong to which insect order?
questions.expl: Diptera (true flies) includes mosquitoes, blackflies, sandflies, and tsetse flies, all medically significant vectors.

questions.q: Sucking lice, vectors of typhus and relapsing fever, belong to which insect order?
questions.expl: Anoplura is the order of sucking lice, vectors of Rickettsia prowazekii (typhus) and relapsing fever.

questions.q: Cockroaches, mechanical vectors of enteric pathogens, belong to which order?
questions.expl: Cockroaches are classified under Dictyoptera and act as mechanical vectors of enteric pathogens.

questions.q: Bees and ants, significant sources of allergens with anaphylaxis risk, belong to which order?
questions.expl: Hymenoptera includes bees and ants, notable for their allergenic potential.

questions.q: Winged insects that undergo metamorphosis are grouped under:
questions.expl: Pterygota refers to winged insects, further subdivided by metamorphosis type into Exopterygota and Endopterygota.

questions.q: In Exopterygota, wings develop:
questions.expl: Exopterygote insects show external wing development, visible even in immature nymphal stages.

questions.q: In Endopterygota, wings develop:
questions.expl: Endopterygote insects develop wings internally during the larval stage, emerging fully formed in the adult.

questions.q: Exopterygota undergo which type of metamorphosis?
questions.expl: Exopterygota undergo gradual (incomplete) metamorphosis, termed hemimetabolism.

questions.q: Complete metamorphosis (holometabolism) is advantageous mainly because:
options: Larvae and adults occupy different niches, avoiding resource competition
Males are eliminated from the population
questions.expl: Endopterygota undergo complete metamorphosis, termed holometabolism.

questions.q: In the five-stage IVM process, what is the purpose of Stage 1 (Situation Analysis & Survey)?
options: To distribute insecticide-treated nets to households
To establish a baseline assessment defining the problem and evidence base
To train community health workers exclusively
questions.expl: Exopterygote immatures are called nymphs — miniature versions of the adult.

questions.q: In Endopterygota, the immature stage is called a:
questions.expl: Endopterygote immatures are called larvae, which occupy a feeding stage distinct from the adult.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of an Exopterygote (hemimetabolous) insect, per the lecture?
questions.expl: Cockroaches, lice, and grasshoppers are given as examples of exopterygote insects with gradual metamorphosis.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of an Endopterygote (holometabolous) insect, per the lecture?
questions.expl: Mosquitoes, flies, beetles, and fleas are given as examples of endopterygote insects with complete metamorphosis.

questions.q: In holometabolous insects such as mosquitoes, the larval stage typically occupies the same habitat as the adult.
questions.expl: Holometabolous larvae and adults often occupy entirely different habitats — mosquito larvae are aquatic while adults are aerial — requiring separate control strategies.

questions.q: The exoskeleton of an insect is made up of:
questions.expl: Hemimetabolous insects progress directly from nymph to adult through successive moults, with no pupal stage.

questions.q: The shedding of the rigid exoskeleton in insects, triggered by hormones, is called:
questions.expl: Ecdysis, or moulting, is the periodic shedding of the old cuticle, digested by moulting fluid and shed along the ecdysial cleavage line.

questions.q: The shed exoskeleton left behind after moulting is referred to as the:
questions.expl: The cast-off skin from moulting is called the exuviae.

questions.q: Each developmental stage or form between successive moults is called a/an:
questions.expl: An instar is the developmental form between two moults; most species pass through 3–4 larval instars.

questions.q: The complete transformation from egg to adult in insects is called:
questions.expl: Metamorphosis describes the full transformation from egg to adult (imago).

questions.q: The reproductively mature adult stage of an insect is also referred to as the:
questions.expl: The adult insect stage is termed the imago, representing the reproductive stage with no further growth.

questions.q: Hatching of the insect egg, marking the start of larval/nymphal life, is termed:
questions.expl: Eclosion marks hatching from the egg, the beginning of the immature developmental stages.

questions.q: Insects possess which type of circulatory system, lacking true veins or arteries?
questions.expl: Insects have an open circulatory system; the haemocoel is filled with haemolymph that bathes tissues directly.

questions.q: The fluid that fills the insect haemocoel and performs the combined functions of blood and lymph is called:
questions.expl: Haemolymph is the colourless fluid filling the haemocoel, performing functions analogous to vertebrate blood and lymph.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a function of insect haemolymph?
options: Carrying excretory products to excretory organs
questions.expl: Insects lack haemoglobin; oxygen delivery occurs via the tracheal system through diffusion, not via haemolymph.

questions.q: The only true blood vessel in insects, comprising a posterior heart and anterior aorta, is the:
questions.expl: The dorsal vessel is the sole true blood vessel, consisting of a pulsating heart posteriorly and an aorta delivering haemolymph to the brain.

questions.q: Valve-like openings in the insect heart that allow haemolymph to enter during diastole are called:
questions.expl: Ostia are valve-like openings in the heart permitting haemolymph entry during diastole.

questions.q: Haemolymph in insects can exert hydraulic pressure that assists processes like wing expansion after moulting.
questions.expl: Haemolymph's mechanical role includes exerting hydraulic pressure that assists wing expansion, appendage extension, and eclosion from the pupal case.

questions.q: The network of internal air tubes through which insects breathe is called the:
questions.expl: Insects breathe via the tracheal system, a network of internal air tubes delivering oxygen directly to tissues.

questions.q: External openings through which air enters the insect tracheal system are called:
questions.expl: Spiracles are the external openings located on the meso- and metathoraces and abdominal segments.

questions.q: The terminal fine tubes of the tracheal system that end directly in cells for gas exchange are called:
questions.expl: Tracheoles are the finest terminal branches of the tracheal system, delivering oxygen directly to individual cells.

questions.q: Spiracle valves open and close primarily to regulate:
questions.expl: Spiracle valves regulate water loss, a critical function in hot, dry environments where conserving moisture is essential.

questions.q: The insect brain is formed by the fusion of how many pairs of ganglia in the head?
questions.expl: Three pairs of ganglia in the head fuse to form the insect brain.

questions.q: Which insect sensory receptors are primarily responsible for taste and smell?
questions.expl: Chemoreceptors, located on antennae and palps, are responsible for taste and smell.

questions.q: Which hormones are highlighted as regulating insect growth, moulting, reproduction, and diapause?
questions.expl: The insect endocrine system relies on hormones including juvenile hormone and ecdysone to regulate development.

questions.q: The insect alimentary canal is divided into how many main regions?
questions.expl: The alimentary canal comprises three regions: foregut, midgut, and hindgut.

questions.q: Which foregut structure stores food temporarily before digestion?
questions.expl: The crop is a foregut storage structure where food is held before further processing.

questions.q: Which region of the insect gut is the primary site of digestion and absorption, lined by the peritrophic membrane?
questions.expl: The midgut is the primary digestion and absorption site, lined by the protective peritrophic membrane.

questions.q: Which structures in the hindgut reabsorb up to 90% of water from the forming faecal pellet?
questions.expl: Rectal papillae in the rectum reabsorb up to 90% of water, a key adaptation for water conservation.

questions.q: In blood-sucking insects, which component of saliva prevents blood clotting at the bite site?
questions.expl: Anticoagulins in saliva prevent clotting, maintaining blood flow during feeding in blood-sucking insects.

questions.q: Which salivary component is responsible for the characteristic itch and wheal of insect bites?
questions.expl: Allergens in saliva trigger local hypersensitivity reactions, producing the itch and wheal typical of insect bites.

questions.q: In most non-blood-feeding insects, saliva primarily moistens the mouthparts and contains digestive enzymes such as amylase.
questions.expl: Saliva normally moistens mouthparts and aids digestion (e.g., amylase in cockroaches); medically significant components like anticoagulins are most prominent in blood-feeding insects.

questions.q: Nitrogenous waste in most insects is excreted primarily in which water-conserving form?
questions.expl: Most insects excrete nitrogenous waste as uric acid, a water-conserving adaptation for terrestrial life.

questions.q: The primary goal of the insect excretory system, achieved mainly via the Malpighian tubules, is to:
options: Maintain a constant internal environment by regulating pH and osmotic concentration
questions.expl: The excretory system maintains homeostasis by regulating the pH and osmotic concentration of the haemolymph.

questions.q: Which structure in the female insect reproductive system stores sperm, enabling fertilization over extended periods from a single mating?
questions.expl: The spermatheca is a muscular pouch that receives and stores sperm, releasing it gradually to fertilize successive egg batches.

questions.q: Accessory glands in the female insect reproductive system primarily secrete materials used for:
options: Waterproofing and adhesive materials for egg pod/shell formation
questions.expl: Female accessory glands secrete waterproof and adhesive materials that protect eggs and fix them to substrates.

questions.q: In male insects, paired structures that produce spermatozoa through spermatogenesis are the:
questions.expl: The testes are paired organs producing spermatozoa via spermatogenesis.

questions.q: In mosquitoes, females typically mate only once and store sufficient sperm for multiple gonotrophic cycles — a consideration relevant to which vector control strategy?
questions.expl: Single mating with long-term sperm storage in mosquitoes is a critical consideration in sterile insect technique (SIT) vector control strategies.

questions.q: Which mode of reproduction, the most common among insects, involves females laying eggs that develop and hatch externally?
questions.expl: Oviparous reproduction, seen in mosquitoes, flies, and beetles, is the most common mode in insects.

questions.q: Which mode of reproduction, exemplified by the tsetse fly (Glossina spp.), involves eggs hatching within the female with larvae nourished internally and born directly?
questions.expl: Viviparous reproduction in tsetse flies is critical for understanding African trypanosomiasis epidemiology, as larvae are nourished internally and born directly.

questions.q: Reproduction from unfertilized ova, seen in social insects like bees where drones arise from unfertilized eggs, is called:
questions.expl: Parthenogenesis, specifically arrhenotoky in bees, produces drones (males) from unfertilized eggs while workers come from fertilized eggs.

questions.q: In honeybees, worker bees develop from unfertilized eggs while drones develop from fertilized eggs.
questions.expl: It is the reverse: worker bees are produced from fertilized eggs, while drones (males) develop from unfertilized eggs (arrhenotoky).

questions.q: Fertilization in insects is internal, with mate-finding commonly mediated by pheromones.
questions.expl: The lecture notes that sexes are almost always separate, fertilization is internal, and pheromones mediate mate finding across distances.

questions.q: To which insect Order do mosquitoes belong?
questions.explain: Mosquitoes belong to the Order Diptera (the 'true flies'), characterised by a single pair of functional wings.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed among the major mosquito genera in the lecture?
questions.explain: The genera listed were Anopheles, Aedes, Culex, Mansonia, Haemagogus and Sabethes. Stegomyia is an older subgenus name sometimes used for Aedes, not one of the genera listed.

questions.q: The hard outer covering of a mosquito's body is called the:

questions.q: Which type of antennae is typically found in FEMALE mosquitoes?

questions.q: What is the function of the maxillary palps?
questions.explain: The maxillary palps are sensory organs that detect odours and can feel objects.

questions.q: Which mosquito mouthpart is the tube-like structure used to suck up fluids?
questions.explain: The proboscis is the tube-like mouthpart used to suck up fluids such as blood or nectar.

questions.q: Which needle-like mouthpart structures penetrate the skin to reach blood vessels?
questions.explain: The maxillae are needle-like structures that penetrate the skin to reach blood vessels.

questions.q: Which stylet probes for and penetrates a blood vessel after the initial incision?
questions.explain: The labrum is the stylet that extends into the incision and probes for and penetrates a blood vessel.

questions.q: Which structure forms a sheath enclosing the other mouthpart stylets and retracts during feeding?
questions.explain: The labium forms a sheath (the visible proboscis casing) that encloses the other stylets and retracts as the stylets penetrate the skin.

questions.q: During feeding, the labium pierces deep into the skin along with the other stylets.
questions.explain: The labium does not pierce the skin; it forms an outer sheath that bends back and retracts while the thinner stylets penetrate the skin.

questions.q: The protective plate sitting on top of the front of the thorax is the:
questions.explain: The antepronotum is a protective plate that sits on top of the front of the thorax.

questions.q: The middle section of the thorax is the:
questions.explain: The scutellum is the middle section of the thorax.

questions.q: Which thoracic structure holds the septum separating the thorax from the abdomen?
questions.explain: The postnotum is the end of the thorax and holds the septum that separates the thorax from the abdomen.

questions.q: The halteres are a true second pair of flight wings used to generate lift.
questions.explain: Halteres are modified hind wings used for balance and steering, not for generating lift; only the front pair of wings is used for flying.

questions.q: How many sections (segments) make up the mosquito abdomen?
questions.explain: The abdomen has 10 sections/segments.

questions.q: Why are the top and bottom of each abdominal segment separated?

options.t: To allow the abdomen to expand with a meal or eggs

questions.explain: The separation between the top and bottom of each segment allows the abdomen to expand when filled with a blood meal or with eggs.

questions.q: The movable parts at the very end of a mosquito's leg are called:
questions.explain: Tarsomeres are the movable parts at the end of the leg.

questions.q: The fourth segment of an insect leg, whose hind version holds the pollen basket, is the:
questions.explain: The tibia is the fourth segment of an insect leg; in the hind leg it holds the pollen basket.

questions.q: The third segment of an insect leg is called the:
questions.explain: The femur is the third segment of an insect leg.

questions.q: Which leg is located farthest from the head?
questions.explain: The hind leg is the leg farthest from the head.

questions.q: Wing thickenings that run along the short axis of the wing are called:
questions.explain: Crossveins are thickenings in the wing that lie along the short axis of the wing.

questions.q: Which of these is given as an example of a 'natural' mosquito breeding habitat?

questions.q: The pupal body is divided into the abdomen and which other fused region?

Very effective but with short residual activity of 2-3 months
