questions.q: How many species/types of lice infest humans, as described in the lecture?
questions.explain: Three types of lice infest humans: the body louse, the head louse, and the pubic louse.

questions.q: Infestation by the body louse is medically termed:
questions.explain: Infestation by Pediculus humanus humanus (the body louse) is called pediculosis corporis.

questions.q: Infestation of the eyelashes by the pubic louse is termed:
questions.explain: When the pubic louse infests the eyelashes, the condition is called pediculosis ciliaris.

questions.q: Lice are described as ectoparasites that live on the surface of their host.
questions.explain: All three types of lice are ectoparasites, living on the surface of the human host rather than inside the body.

questions.q: What is the host range of human lice?
questions.explain: All three types of human lice have humans as their only host.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a common name for the body louse mentioned in the lecture?
questions.explain: The body louse is called the clothing louse, gray back, or mechanized dandruff. 'Wall louse' is actually a nickname for the bed bug.

questions.q: Why is the body louse wingless?

options.t: Its wings were lost through injury
As an evolutionary adaptation to its ectoparasitic lifestyle
It never had wings as an insect order trait

questions.explain: Winglessness in the body louse is described as an adaptation suited to life as a permanent ectoparasite.

questions.q: How many segments make up the body louse's antennae?
questions.explain: The body louse has short, 5-segmented antennae.

questions.q: How many pairs of legs does the body louse have, and how are they described?
questions.explain: The body louse has 3 pairs of legs that are stout and well developed, suited for gripping hair/clothing fibres.

questions.q: How many segments make up the abdomen of the body louse?
questions.explain: The body louse abdomen has 9 segments with sclerotised (hardened) lateral margins.

questions.q: Where are spiracles found on the body louse?
questions.explain: Spiracles (breathing openings) are present on both the thorax and abdomen of the body louse.

questions.q: Which structure of the louse mouthparts has tiny teeth and helps anchor it to the skin?
questions.explain: The labrum bears tiny teeth that help the louse grip the skin during feeding.

questions.q: The pouch that houses the louse's piercing 'stabbing apparatus' is called the:
questions.explain: The stylet sac contains the stabbing apparatus (the piercing stylets) used during feeding.

questions.q: How many ventral maxillae stylets does the louse possess?
questions.explain: The louse has 2 ventral maxillae stylets, which work alongside the mandible and hypopharynx.

questions.q: Compared with the body and head louse, the pubic louse is:
questions.explain: The pubic louse is smaller than the other two types of lice.

questions.q: Which pair(s) of legs in the pubic louse bear massive claws?
questions.explain: The 2nd and 3rd pairs of legs have massive claws, while the 1st pair is small and slender.

questions.q: What are the three general life stages of lice?
questions.explain: The general lice life cycle stages are egg/nit, nymph (with several molts), and adult.

questions.q: Only adult lice take blood meals; nymphs do not feed on blood.
questions.explain: Both nymphs and adults take blood meals from the human host.

questions.q: How are louse nits typically described in shape and colour?
questions.explain: Louse nits are oval and white, and possess a small lid called an operculum.

questions.q: Louse eggs are laid loosely and can easily fall off the hair or clothing.
questions.explain: Louse eggs are firmly cemented/glued into place on hair shafts or clothing fibres, which is why they are hard to remove.

questions.q: How long does the general louse egg stage last before hatching?
questions.explain: The general louse egg stage lasts 6-10 days before hatching.

questions.q: When do body lice typically feed on their human host?
questions.explain: Body lice feeding occurs both day and night.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a factor that attracts body lice to a host?
questions.explain: Body lice are attracted by odour, sweat chemistry, body temperature, humidity, and darkness (e.g. beneath clothing) - not bright light.

questions.q: Body lice are described as 'gregarious', meaning they are typically found:

options.t: Clustered together, e.g. in clothing seams

questions.explain: Body lice are gregarious, commonly found clustered together in the seams of clothing.

questions.q: The body louse life cycle, involving gradual development without a pupal stage, is described as:
questions.explain: Lice undergo incomplete metamorphosis, developing through nymphal instars rather than a pupal stage.

questions.q: How long does it take a body louse to reach full maturity from hatching?
questions.explain: Body lice reach maturity in 16-27 days.

questions.q: Adult body lice are described as very sensitive to body temperature.
questions.explain: Adult body lice are very sensitive to body temperature, which influences their feeding and movement behaviour.

questions.q: According to the head lice life cycle diagram, what is the egg laid on a hair shaft called?
questions.explain: An egg laid on a hair shaft is called a 'nit', as shown in the head lice life cycle diagram.

questions.q: According to the head lice life cycle diagram, when does the first moult occur after hatching?
questions.explain: The first moult occurs 2 days after hatching, according to the head lice life cycle diagram.

questions.q: According to the head lice life cycle diagram, when does the third moult occur after hatching?
questions.explain: The third moult occurs 10 days after hatching, after which the louse emerges as an adult.

questions.q: According to the head lice life cycle diagram, roughly how many eggs does the female lay per day for the next 16 days after her first egg?
questions.explain: The female lays approximately 4 to 8 eggs per day for the next 16 days.

questions.q: How is the general biology of the head louse described relative to the body louse?

options.t: Aquatic compared to the terrestrial body louse

questions.explain: The head louse is described as similar to the body louse in its biology.

questions.q: Approximately how many eggs does a female head louse lay per day?
questions.explain: The female head louse lays about 6-8 eggs per day.

questions.q: Approximately how many eggs does a female head louse lay over her lifetime?
questions.explain: A female head louse lays about 300 eggs over her lifetime.

questions.q: How many nymphal instars does the head louse undergo, similar to other lice?
questions.explain: The head louse, like the other human lice, undergoes 3 nymphal instars.

questions.q: Approximately how many eggs does a female pubic louse lay over her lifetime?
questions.explain: A female pubic louse lays about 200 eggs over her lifetime.

questions.q: What type of atmosphere does the pubic louse prefer?
questions.explain: The pubic louse prefers a humid atmosphere.

questions.q: What is the primary mode of transmission for the pubic louse?
questions.explain: Pubic louse infestation occurs primarily through sexual contact.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT listed as an epidemiological factor associated with body louse infestation?
questions.explain: Body louse epidemiology is linked to poverty, poor hygiene, and crowding - not high altitude.

questions.q: Which population group is most commonly affected by head lice?
questions.explain: Children are most commonly affected by head lice infestation.

questions.q: Roughly how many nits per day does a female head louse cement to hair, according to the epidemiology section?
questions.explain: In the epidemiology section, the female head louse is described as living 1 month and laying 7-10 nits per day.

questions.q: How is pubic louse transmission via fomites (inanimate objects) described, compared to sexual transmission?
questions.explain: Transmission of the pubic louse via fomites is considered less likely compared to sexual transmission.

questions.q: Approximately how many nits per day does the female pubic louse lay, and for how long does she live?
questions.explain: The female pubic louse lives about 3-4 weeks, laying approximately 3 nits per day.

questions.q: What is the general complaint associated with head louse infestation?
questions.explain: The general complaint with head louse infestation is the itch (pruritus).

questions.q: Where does itching occur in pubic louse infestation?

options.t: Only in infested areas of the body

questions.explain: Itching from pubic lice occurs only in the areas of the body that are infested.

questions.q: Besides the pubic area, to which of these sites can pubic lice spread?

options.t: Eyelashes, moustache, beard, chest, thighs, umbilicus
Only the soles of the feet

questions.explain: Pubic lice may spread from the pubic area to the perineum, thighs, umbilicus, chest, moustache, beard, and eyelashes.

questions.q: How long do mosquitoes typically take to develop from egg to adult?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which secondary bacterial skin infection is mentioned as a complication of body louse infestation?
questions.explain: Secondary bacterial infections such as impetigo may complicate body louse infestation.

questions.q: Louse-borne relapsing fever is caused by which organism?
questions.explain: Louse-borne relapsing fever is caused by the bacterium Borrelia recurrentis.

questions.q: Louse-borne relapsing fever is also known by which alternative name?
questions.explain: Louse-borne borreliosis is also known as Epidemic Relapsing Fever.

questions.q: How does a body louse typically transmit the relapsing fever organism to a new host?

options.t: Only when the louse is crushed/injured, e.g. during scratching
Through louse eggs hatching on skin

questions.explain: The relapsing fever organism infects a new host only when the louse is injured, such as during scratching, releasing the organism from the louse's body.

questions.q: What behaviour do body lice exhibit when their host develops a fever?

options.t: They leave the febrile host to seek a host with normal temperature
They burrow deeper into the skin

questions.explain: Body lice tend to leave a host that develops a fever, moving on to seek a host with normal body temperature - aiding disease spread.

questions.q: How is louse-borne typhus typically transmitted to a person, following a louse bite?

options.t: Directly through louse saliva during the bite
By autoinoculation of louse faeces through scratching the bite site

questions.explain: After a louse bites and ingests bacteraemic blood, the organism multiplies in its gut and is excreted in faeces; the person then autoinoculates themselves by scratching the bite.

questions.q: Untreated cases of louse-borne typhus may die as a result of:

options.t: Peripheral vascular collapse or bacterial pneumonia

questions.explain: Untreated typhus cases may die from peripheral vascular collapse or bacterial pneumonia.

questions.q: Trench fever is typically fatal, with a high mortality rate.
questions.explain: Trench fever is described as not fatal, although it can be incapacitating.

questions.q: Which insecticide dust historically used for head louse treatment is mentioned in the lecture?
questions.explain: DDT-based shampoos/dust are mentioned as part of historical head louse treatment.

questions.q: Besides insecticidal shampoos, which other physical method is mentioned for head louse removal?
questions.explain: Hot combs are mentioned as a physical method used in head louse removal, along with shaving in severe cases.

questions.q: Bed bugs belong to which insect Order?
questions.explain: Bed bugs belong to the Order Hemiptera (the 'true bugs').

questions.q: Which bed bug species is known as the 'human bed bug' and has cosmopolitan distribution, found mainly in temperate zones?
questions.explain: Cimex lectularius is the human bed bug, found mainly in temperate zones, with cosmopolitan distribution.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a nickname for bed bugs mentioned in the lecture?
questions.explain: Bed bugs are nicknamed 'red coats', 'mahogany flats', and 'wall louse'. 'Mechanized dandruff' is actually a nickname for the body louse.

questions.q: How is the bed bug's feeding habit best classified?
questions.explain: Bed bugs are obligate haematophagous insects, meaning they must feed on blood.

questions.q: What is the general body shape of the adult bed bug?
questions.explain: Adult bed bugs have an oval body shape.

questions.q: What colour is an unfed adult bed bug typically?
questions.explain: An unfed adult bed bug is typically pale yellow to brown in colour.

questions.q: Like the body louse, the bed bug's body is flattened in which orientation?
questions.explain: Bed bugs are flattened dorsoventrally, similar to the body louse, allowing them to hide in narrow cracks.

questions.q: How is the bed bug's head generally shaped?
questions.explain: The bed bug head is short and broad.

questions.q: How many segments make up the bed bug's antennae?
questions.explain: The bed bug has 4-segmented antennae.

questions.q: Which thoracic segment is the largest in the bed bug?

options.t: All segments are equal in size

questions.explain: The prothorax is larger than the mesothorax and metathorax in bed bugs.

questions.q: Where do the rudimentary, non-functional wings of the bed bug lie?

options.t: They are entirely absent, with no trace

questions.explain: The rudimentary, non-functional wings (hemielytra) of the bed bug lie over the meso- and metathorax.

questions.q: What shape is the bed bug's abdomen often compared to?
questions.explain: The bed bug's abdomen is described as lemon shaped.

questions.q: In the male bed bug, the abdomen bears a well-developed structure used in mating, the:
questions.explain: The male bed bug has a well-developed, curved penis on the abdomen.

questions.q: When are bed bugs most active in feeding on blood?
questions.explain: Both sexes of bed bugs feed on blood especially at night, when they are most active.

questions.q: Bed bugs are described as 'gregarious', meaning they tend to:
questions.explain: Bed bugs are gregarious in nature, often found aggregated together in harbourages.

questions.q: What colour and shape are bed bug eggs typically described as?
questions.explain: Bed bug eggs are whitish/yellow, curved anteriorly, and vase shaped.

questions.q: What structure on the bed bug egg is pushed open during hatching?
questions.explain: The bed bug egg has a small lid called an operculum, which is pushed open as the nymph hatches.

questions.q: How long does it take for bed bug eggs to hatch?
questions.explain: Bed bug eggs hatch after 8-11 days.

questions.q: The bed bug life cycle, involving nymphal stages without a true pupa, is classified as:

options.t: Paurometabolous only in nymphs, not adults

questions.explain: The bed bug life cycle is hemimetabolous (incomplete metamorphosis), as in lice.

questions.q: What is required for each bed bug nymphal instar to progress to the next stage?
questions.explain: Each nymphal instar requires at least one blood meal before it can moult to the next stage.

questions.q: Approximately how long does the bed bug nymphal period last in total?
questions.explain: The bed bug nymphal period lasts approximately 5-8 weeks.

questions.q: Approximately how long can adult bed bugs live?
questions.explain: Adult bed bugs can live for relatively long periods, approximately 1-4 years.

questions.q: Bed bugs have a low tolerance for desiccation (drying out) and die quickly in dry conditions.
questions.explain: Bed bugs can semi-hibernate and actually have a high desiccation tolerance, contributing to their resilience.

questions.q: Where is sperm stored in the female bed bug following traumatic insemination?
questions.explain: Sperm is stored in the spermatheca (copulatory pouch) of the female bed bug.

questions.q: What characteristic odour is associated with a heavy bed bug infestation?
questions.explain: A heavy bed bug infestation may produce a sickly sweet smell, likened to rotting raspberries.

questions.q: Why do bed bugs typically defecate on bedding rather than on clothing?

options.t: They do not tarry on clothes
They cannot digest while on clothing

questions.explain: Bed bugs do not tarry on clothes, so they tend to defecate on bedding instead, where they rest longer.

questions.q: Bed bugs are confirmed natural vectors of at least one major human disease.
questions.explain: Bed bugs are not considered natural vectors of any human disease, despite their bites causing discomfort.

questions.q: The medical condition resulting from bed bug bites is termed:
questions.explain: Bed bug bites cause a condition termed Cimicosis.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a symptom/effect associated with bed bug bites?
questions.explain: Bed bug bites are associated with distress, anaemia, nervousness, insomnia, nausea, vomiting, chills, and iron deficiency in children - not joint deformity.

questions.q: Sealing cracks, crevices, and gaps in a building to prevent bed bug harbourage is an example of:
questions.explain: Sealing cracks and crevices to deny bed bugs hiding places is a form of structure proofing.

questions.q: Which of these is listed as an additional bed bug control measure besides structure proofing and chemical control?
questions.explain: Impregnated bed nets are listed as another control method against bed bugs.

questions.q: What is recommended for mattresses during bed bug elimination?

options.t: Spray/soak with insecticide and cover with mattress encasements over seams and folds
Leave mattresses untouched, treat only the frame

questions.explain: Mattresses should be sprayed or soaked with insecticide and then covered with large encasements over the seams and folds.

questions.q: What is recommended for heavily infested carpets that cannot be treated effectively?

options.t: Cover them with a rug only
Vacuum them, or discard and burn them

questions.explain: Carpets should be vacuumed, and heavily infested carpets may need to be discarded and burned.

questions.q: Sandflies belong to which family?
questions.explain: Sandflies are in the family Psychodidae, sub-order Nematocera, order Diptera.

questions.q: The medically important subfamily of sandflies is:
questions.explain: Phlebotominae is the blood-feeding subfamily — hence the term 'phlebotomine sandfly'.

questions.q: Approximately how many species of phlebotomine sandflies exist?
questions.explain: There are about 700 species of phlebotomine sandflies.

questions.q: How many sandfly species are anthropophagous (bite humans)?
questions.explain: Only about 90 of the 700 species are anthropophagous, so most sandflies are of no medical importance.

questions.q: Which sandfly genus transmits leishmaniasis in the New World?
questions.explain: Lutzomyia is the New World vector genus.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT an Old World sandfly genus?
questions.explain: Lutzomyia is a New World genus; Phlebotomus, Sergentomyia and Chinius occur in the Old World.

questions.q: The Duffy antigen in humans affects susceptibility to which disease?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: What is the length of an adult sandfly?
questions.explain: Adult sandflies are tiny, 1.5–3.5 mm long.

questions.q: Which feature is characteristic of the sandfly?

options.t: Hairy appearance with large black eyes and long legs

questions.explain: Sandflies are hairy with large black eyes and long legs.

questions.q: Sandfly locomotion is characterised by:
questions.explain: Sandflies show a characteristic jumping/hopping flight.

questions.q: Sandfly eggs hatch after:
questions.explain: Eggs hatch after 4–20 days.

questions.q: Sandfly larval development is completed after:
questions.explain: Larval development takes 20–30 days through four instars.

questions.q: The sandfly pupal stage lasts:
questions.explain: The pupal stage lasts 6–13 days before the adult emerges.

questions.q: Sandfly larvae feed as:
questions.explain: Sandfly larvae are scavengers; larval diapause can occur due to temperature and nutrient availability.

questions.q: Which statement about sandfly eggs is CORRECT?

options.t: They are laid on the water surface
They are laid in water but need oxygen
They are laid inside the host's skin
They require high humidity but are NOT laid in water

questions.explain: Sandfly eggs need a high-humidity microhabitat but are not laid in water — a key difference from mosquitoes.

questions.q: Sandflies feed by:

options.t: Creating a pool of blood and feeding from it

questions.explain: Sandflies are pool feeders: mouthparts probe the skin creating a pool of blood from which they feed.

questions.q: Most sandfly species feed:

options.t: At dusk and during the night

questions.explain: Most species feed at dusk and at night, when temperature falls and humidity rises.

questions.q: How many eggs does a female sandfly lay per gonotrophic cycle?
questions.explain: Females lay 30–70 eggs per gonotrophic cycle.

questions.q: Sandflies locate mates with the aid of:
questions.explain: Males locate females at resting sites or on hosts with the aid of pheromones.

questions.q: In urban and peri-urban settings, the main sandfly targets are:
questions.explain: In urban and peri-urban areas humans and domestic dogs are the main targets — and the dog is also a reservoir host.

questions.q: Why is control of immature sandfly stages difficult?

options.t: The breeding sites of most species are unknown
Larvae are resistant to all insecticides
Larvae only develop in treated water

questions.explain: Control of immature stages is difficult because the breeding sites of most species are unknown.

questions.q: Which biological agent reduces survival and fecundity of phlebotomine sandflies?
questions.explain: Bacillus sphaericus has been shown to reduce survival and fecundity of phlebotomine sandflies.

questions.q: Leishmania parasites are best described as:

options.t: Intracellular parasites of blood and tissues

questions.explain: Leishmania are intracellular parasites of both blood and tissues, living inside macrophages.

questions.q: The form of Leishmania found in humans is the:
questions.explain: Amastigotes occur in humans and other vertebrates; promastigotes occur in the sandfly's intestine.

questions.q: The form of Leishmania found in the sandfly intestine is the:
questions.explain: Promastigotes are found in the intestine of the sandfly.

questions.q: Leishmaniasis affects approximately how many people worldwide?
questions.explain: Leishmaniasis is a zoonotic infection affecting about 12 million people worldwide in 88 countries.

questions.q: Leishmaniasis is reported in how many countries?
questions.explain: It occurs in 88 countries.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the four main Leishmania species of medical importance?
questions.explain: The four main species listed are L. tropica, L. braziliensis, L. mexicana and L. donovani. L. major is another cause of cutaneous disease but is not one of the four main species listed.

questions.q: The size of a Leishmania amastigote is approximately:
questions.explain: Amastigotes are small round-oval bodies 2–4 µm depending on species.

questions.q: In stained smears, the nucleus and kinetoplast of an amastigote stain:
questions.explain: Nucleus and kinetoplast stain dark reddish-mauve while the cytoplasm stains palely.

questions.q: Amastigotes are typically seen:
questions.explain: They are seen in groups inside macrophages, or lying freely between cells.

questions.q: After a sandfly injects promastigotes into skin, they:

options.t: Lose their flagella and become amastigotes

questions.explain: Promastigotes lose their flagella to become amastigotes, which are then taken up by macrophages.

questions.q: Leishmania tropica causes:
questions.explain: L. tropica causes cutaneous leishmaniasis, also called Oriental sore.

questions.q: The reservoir hosts of Leishmania tropica include:
questions.explain: Reservoir hosts are dogs, foxes and rodents.

questions.q: The first lesion of cutaneous leishmaniasis is:

options.t: A red papule at the bite site

questions.explain: A red papule appears at the site of the bite, becomes itchy, enlarges and ulcerates.

questions.q: Lesions of cutaneous leishmaniasis typically:
questions.explain: Lesions may heal in a few months but leave disfiguring scars.

questions.q: Leishmania braziliensis causes:
questions.explain: L. braziliensis causes mucocutaneous leishmaniasis (chiclero ulcer).

questions.q: Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis spreads from the bite site via the:
questions.explain: There is metastatic spread of promastigotes via the lymphatics, involving nose, pharynx, palate and lips.

questions.q: Invasion of the pharynx in mucocutaneous leishmaniasis may result in:
questions.explain: Invasion of the pharynx may result in loss of speech, with severe disfiguring and facial mutilation.

questions.q: The term 'kala-azar' means:
questions.explain: Advanced disease darkens the skin; kala-azar means black fever.

questions.q: The incubation period of visceral leishmaniasis is:
questions.explain: The incubation period is several weeks to 1 year.

questions.q: Untreated chronic visceral leishmaniasis usually leads to death within:
questions.explain: Chronic cases usually lead to death in 1–2 years if not treated.

questions.q: Leishmania is cultured in which medium?
questions.explain: Tissue specimens or blood are cultured in NNN medium.

questions.q: The Montenegro test is also known as the:
questions.explain: The Leishmanin skin test is also called the Montenegro test.

questions.q: The drug of choice for visceral leishmaniasis is:
questions.explain: Pentavalent antimonials — sodium stibogluconate (20 mg/kg daily for 28 days) and meglumine antimoniate — are the drugs of choice.

questions.q: Which is NOT used to treat leishmaniasis?
questions.explain: Permethrin is a topical scabicide/insecticide, not a treatment for leishmaniasis.

questions.q: The scabies mite is:
questions.explain: Sarcoptes scabiei is the scabies mite, a permanent ectoparasite of human skin.

questions.q: Scabies is also known as:
questions.explain: Diseases caused are scabies, acariasis or Norwegian itch.

questions.q: How many pairs of legs does an adult scabies mite have?
questions.explain: Arachnids have four pairs of legs; insects have three.

questions.q: The 'false head' at the anterior of the idiosoma is the:
questions.explain: The capitulum is the false head at the anterior part of the idiosoma.

questions.q: Which structures are ABSENT in the scabies mite?
questions.explain: There are no maxillae, no mandibles and no hypopharynx.

questions.q: The size of an adult scabies mite is:
questions.explain: Adults are 0.3–0.5 mm, scarcely visible to the naked eye.

questions.q: The dorsal spines of the scabies mite point:
questions.explain: Peg-like protuberances (dorsal spines) point backwards over the body, helping the mite move forward in its burrow.

questions.q: In the FEMALE scabies mite, the 3rd and 4th pairs of legs end in:
questions.explain: In females the first two pairs end in a stalk (pedicel) with suckers; the 3rd and 4th pairs end in long bristles.

questions.q: Each scabies mite leg is divided into how many ring-like segments?
questions.explain: The four pairs of brown stumpy legs are divided into five ring-like segments.

questions.q: The female scabies mite burrows in which skin layer?
questions.explain: Females excavate thin tortuous tunnels in the epidermis, specifically the stratum corneum.

questions.q: How long does it take a scabies mite to disappear into the skin?
questions.explain: It takes about 2–20 minutes, depending on ambient temperature.

questions.q: Where is the female mite normally found in the tunnel?
questions.explain: The female feeds on liquids from destroyed cells and is normally found at the blind end of the tunnel.

questions.q: How many eggs does a female scabies mite lay per day?
questions.explain: Oval-shaped eggs are laid 2–3 a day; the female lives about 1–2 months.

questions.q: Scabies eggs hatch in:
questions.explain: Eggs hatch in 3–5 days into a six-legged larva (hexapod).

questions.q: The scabies nymph has how many legs?
questions.explain: After 2–3 days the larva moults into an eight-legged nymph (octopod).

questions.q: What happens to the male scabies mite after copulation?
questions.explain: Copulation occurs only between an adult male and adult female, and males die after copulation.

questions.q: Which is a recognised risk factor for scabies?
questions.explain: Risk factors include intrafamilial contact, overcrowding, lack of water supply and sexual promiscuity.

questions.q: The itching in scabies is caused by:
questions.explain: Itching is caused by toxic secretions and faecal particles — an allergic reaction — and is intense at night.

questions.q: The commonest secondary bacterial infection in scabies is:
questions.explain: Scabies often leads to secondary bacterial infection, especially impetigo, plus eczema, boils and pustules.

questions.q: Crusted (Norwegian) scabies is most common in:

options.t: People with weakened immune systems, the elderly and the disabled

questions.explain: Crusted scabies involves tens of thousands of mites and occurs mainly in the immunosuppressed, elderly and disabled. It is highly contagious.

questions.q: Items that cannot be washed should be sealed in a plastic bag for:
questions.explain: Unwashable items should be placed in a sealed plastic bag for seven days.

questions.q: Which drug is given ORALLY for scabies?
questions.explain: Ivermectin is given as an oral dose; benzyl benzoate, permethrin and sulphur are topical.

questions.q: After starting scabies treatment, patients can usually return to school or work after:
questions.explain: Medication kills mites and eggs quickly and patients can usually return after 24 hours, though itching may persist for weeks.

questions.q: Why should hydrocortisone cream be used cautiously in scabies?

options.t: It kills the mites too fast
It causes the mite to burrow deeper
It is toxic to the liver
It changes the appearance of the rash, making diagnosis harder

questions.explain: Hydrocortisone may relieve itching but alters the rash appearance, so it is best used only after the diagnosis is confirmed.

questions.q: Tsetse flies belong to which genus?
questions.explain: Tsetse flies are bloodsucking flies of the genus Glossina.

questions.q: Tsetse flies occur:
questions.explain: Tsetse flies occur only in tropical Africa.

questions.q: Sleeping sickness occurs in:
questions.explain: Sleeping sickness occurs in Africa south of the Sahara.

questions.q: Approximately how many people die of sleeping sickness each year?
questions.explain: 20,000 to 25,000 people die each year.

questions.q: Adult tsetse flies measure:
questions.explain: Tsetse flies are robust, 6–15 mm in length.

questions.q: Tsetse flies are distinguished from other biting flies by:

options.t: Forward-pointing mouthparts and characteristic wing venation

questions.explain: They are distinguished by forward-pointing mouthparts (proboscis) and characteristic wing venation.

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the three tsetse subgenera?
questions.explain: The three subgenera are Austenia (G. fusca group), Nemorhina (G. palpalis group) and Glossina (G. morsitans group).

questions.q: The G. palpalis group belongs to which subgenus?
questions.explain: Nemorhina is the G. palpalis group.

questions.q: The G. fusca group belongs to which subgenus?
questions.explain: Austenia is the G. fusca group.

questions.q: How many species and subspecies of tsetse are known to transmit sleeping sickness?
questions.explain: Only nine species and subspecies, belonging to the G. palpalis or G. morsitans groups, transmit sleeping sickness.

questions.q: Which tsetse group is NOT known to transmit sleeping sickness?
questions.explain: Only the G. palpalis and G. morsitans groups transmit sleeping sickness — the G. fusca group does not.

questions.q: Which mode of reproduction, exemplified by the tsetse fly (Glossina spp.), involves eggs hatching within the female with larvae nourished internally and born directly?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Where does the tsetse larva develop?
questions.explain: The egg develops into a larva within the mother's uterus, where it is fed by milk glands.

questions.q: The tsetse larva is nourished inside the mother by:
questions.explain: The larva hatches in the uterus after about 4 days and is fed by 'milk glands' as it develops.

questions.q: How often does a female tsetse deposit a larva?
questions.explain: The mother produces a single larva at roughly nine-day intervals (7–11 days) for her entire life.

questions.q: What does the tsetse larva do after being deposited?

options.t: Burrows into the ground and pupates

questions.explain: The larva burrows 1.5–2 cm into the ground where it forms a puparium and pupates.

questions.q: How deep does the tsetse larva burrow?
questions.explain: The larva burrows 1.5–2 cm underground.

questions.q: The adult tsetse emerges from the pupa after about:
questions.explain: The adult fly emerges from the pupa in the ground after about 30 days.

questions.q: How many days elapse between emergence of one female tsetse and the emergence of her first offspring?
questions.explain: About 50 days elapse between the emergence of one female fly and the emergence of the first of its progeny.

questions.q: Tsetse larvae deposited on the ground are:
questions.explain: The female deposits a third instar larva, generally 3–8.5 mm long with two black knobs at the posterior end.

questions.q: Which parasite listed in the lecture is the causative agent of African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness)?
questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Animal African Trypanosomiasis is also known as:
questions.explain: Animal African Trypanosomiasis is called Nagana.

questions.q: Which trypanosome is most prevalent in cattle and small ruminants?
questions.explain: Trypanosoma congolense is the most prevalent species affecting cattle and small ruminants.

questions.q: Trypanosoma simiae causes particularly virulent disease in:
questions.explain: Trypanosoma simiae causes a particularly virulent disease in pigs.

questions.q: In the human, trypanosomes multiply by:
questions.explain: Trypomastigotes multiply by binary fission in body fluids such as blood, lymph and spinal fluid.

questions.q: In the tsetse fly, bloodstream trypomastigotes first transform into:
questions.explain: Bloodstream trypomastigotes become procyclic trypomastigotes in the vector midgut and multiply by binary fission.

questions.q: Where do epimastigotes multiply in the tsetse fly?
questions.explain: Epimastigotes multiply in the salivary gland and transform into metacyclic trypomastigotes.

questions.q: Which animals are reservoirs for T. b. rhodesiense?
questions.explain: Cattle and possibly wild ungulates are reservoirs for T. b. rhodesiense.

questions.q: The earliest clinical sign of sleeping sickness is often:

options.t: Swelling of lymph glands near the bite

questions.explain: Initially the lymph glands near the bite often become swollen.

questions.q: Which is NOT a feature of progressing sleeping sickness?
questions.explain: Progression brings spleen enlargement, oedema, endocrine disorders, impotence, abortion, sleeplessness and rash.

questions.q: Which symptom gives sleeping sickness its name?
questions.explain: Excessive sleeping, part of the meningoencephalitis picture, gives the disease its name.

questions.q: Untreated sleeping sickness finally leads to:
questions.explain: If untreated, coma may develop leading finally to death.

questions.q: Which tsetse control method exploits the fact that females mate only once?
questions.explain: The sterile male insect technique is used especially during the eradication phase — if a female's single mating is with a sterile male she remains barren.

questions.q: Which is NOT a listed tsetse control method?
questions.explain: Control methods include traps, odour baits and targets, insecticide on livestock, ground and aerial spraying, sterile males and bush clearing. There is no vaccine.

questions.q: Insecticide can be applied to livestock by:
questions.explain: Insecticide application on livestock is done through spraying, dipping and pour-on.

questions.q: Biting midges belong to which family?
questions.explain: Biting midges are in the family Ceratopogonidae, sub-order Nematocera, order Diptera.

questions.q: Which is NOT a genus of biting midge?
questions.explain: The genera are Culicoides, Leptoconops and Lasiohelea. Phlebotomus is a sandfly.

questions.q: Biting midges are commonly called:
questions.explain: They are called 'no-see-ums' because they are the smallest man-biting insect and move in swarms.

questions.q: The adult biting midge measures:
questions.explain: At 1.5–3 mm, Culicoides is the smallest man-biting insect.

questions.q: Biting midge antennae have how many segments?
questions.explain: The bead-like antennae have 15 segments, characteristic of the sub-order Nematocera.

questions.q: The mouthparts of a biting midge are:
questions.explain: Mouthparts are inconspicuous and dagger-like, resembling those of the black fly.

questions.q: What is the most diagnostic visual feature of the genus Aedes, especially Ae. aegypti?

options.t: Black-and-white silvery scale banding, including a lyre-shaped thoracic pattern
A single red stripe down the abdomen
Plain brown coloration with no markings

questions.explain: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Biting midge wings are:

options.t: Short and broad with dark and white patches

questions.explain: Wings are short and broad with dark and white patches, and are crossed over the body at rest.

questions.q: At rest, the wings of a biting midge are:
questions.explain: The patterned wings are crossed at rest — unlike the sandfly, which holds its wings erect.

questions.q: The abdomen of a biting midge has how many segments?
questions.explain: The abdomen is 9-segmented; males show prominent claspers.

questions.q: Biting midges are described as crepuscular, meaning they are active:
questions.explain: They are basically crepuscular insects, very active just before 7 pm.

questions.q: Biting midges are exophilic, meaning they:
questions.explain: Being exophilic (outdoor-resting), indoor insecticide spraying is largely ineffective against them.

questions.q: Biting midge eggs are:
questions.explain: Eggs are small and ovoid, about 0.5 mm, black or brown and banana-shaped.

questions.q: Biting midge eggs are laid in batches of:

options.t: A single egg at a time

questions.explain: Eggs are laid in batches of 30 to 250–450.

questions.q: Biting midge eggs hatch in:
questions.explain: Eggs hatch in 2–9 days, depending on species and temperature.

questions.q: The biting midge larva has how many visible segments?
questions.explain: There are 12 visible but similar segments — 3 thoracic and 9 abdominal.

questions.q: A distinctive feature of the biting midge larva is that it is:

options.t: Devoid of any hairs or bristles

questions.explain: The larva has no hairs or bristles — it is devoid of any surface structure.

questions.q: The biting midge larva bears which structures on the terminal abdominal segment?
questions.explain: There are 2 four-lobed retractile gills on the terminal abdominal segment.

questions.q: Biting midge larvae feed as:
questions.explain: Larvae are scavengers with a characteristic serpentine movement.

questions.q: How many larval instars do biting midges have?
questions.explain: There are 4 larval instars; some species have a proleg to help with movement.

questions.q: Which is a recognised biting midge larval habitat?

options.t: Tree holes, marshy areas and horse/cow manure

questions.explain: Larval habitats include tree holes, marshy/boggy/swampy areas and horse or cow manure.

questions.q: The biting midge pupa resembles that of a:
questions.explain: The pupa resembles a mosquito pupa, with two prominent segmented breathing trumpets.

questions.q: The biting midge pupa is found in:

options.t: The drier areas of their habitat

questions.explain: Unlike mosquito pupae, biting midge pupae are found in drier areas of the habitat.

questions.q: The biting midge pupal period lasts:
questions.explain: The pupal period is 3–10 days.

questions.q: Biting midge bites cause:

options.t: Painless swelling that resolves in minutes
Intense itching and welts that persist a long time

questions.explain: Bites cause intense itching and long-persisting welts — an allergic reaction.

questions.q: Dipetalonema perstans causes dermatitis mainly in:
questions.explain: Dipetalonema perstans causes dermatitis and occurs in East Africa.

questions.q: Which Culicoides species transmits Dipetalonema streptocerca?
questions.explain: C. grahamii is the vector of D. streptocerca in West African rainforest areas.

questions.q: Microfilariae transmitted by biting midges are:
questions.explain: They are non-periodic, so blood samples can be taken at any time of day — unlike Wuchereria.

questions.q: Microfilariae transmitted by biting midges are described as:
questions.explain: They are non-pathogenic but cause morbidity and allergic reactions in man.

questions.q: Where do microfilariae moult in the biting midge vector?
questions.explain: Microfilariae moult twice in the thoracic muscles of the vector.

questions.q: Why is control of biting midges difficult?

options.t: They breed only in treated water
They are resistant to all insecticides
Their habitats are diffuse and extensive

questions.explain: Habitats such as fresh and salt water marshes and wet coastlands are diffuse and extensive, making reduction laborious and impractical.

questions.q: Which organochlorines have been used against biting midges?
questions.explain: Organochlorines such as dieldrin and DDT have been used.

questions.q: Screens used against biting midges must be:
questions.explain: Screens with small mesh are needed because ordinary mesh lets a 1.5 mm midge straight through.

questions.q: Which attractant is used in insecticide-treated targets for biting midges?
questions.explain: Removal trapping and insecticide-treated targets use carbon dioxide as an attractant.

questions.q: Biting midges are a particular threat to which industry?
questions.explain: Swarming midges are a genuine threat to the tourist industry, especially in Europe and the Americas.

questions.q: Hard ticks belong to which class, order, and family?
options: Class Insecta, Order Diptera, Family Culicidae
Class Arachnida, Order Metastigmata, Family Ixodidae
Class Arachnida, Order Araneae, Family Ixodidae
Class Crustacea, Order Metastigmata, Family Argasidae
questions.expl: Hard ticks are classified as Class Arachnida, Order Metastigmata, Sub-order Ixodida, Family Ixodidae, comprising 9 genera.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT listed as an example genus/species of hard tick?
questions.expl: Ornithodoros moubata is a soft tick (family Argasidae, the African relapsing fever tick), not a hard tick.

questions.q: Why are Ixodid ticks referred to as "hard" ticks?
options: Because their bites are extremely painful
Because they can resist the force of a human foot
Because they only live in hard, rocky soil
Because they lack a digestive system
questions.expl: Hard ticks are called "hard" because they can resist the force of human feet, owing to their sclerotized dorsal shield.

questions.q: Which statement about hard tick bites and habitat is TRUE?
options: Bites are typically very painful and ticks prefer dry habitats
Bites are typically painless and ticks thrive in areas of high humidity
Bites are painless but ticks avoid humid environments
Ticks cannot detect their hosts at all
questions.expl: Hard tick bites are painless, and ticks thrive in areas with high humidity, often congregating in tight clumps.

questions.q: How do hard ticks primarily detect a potential host?
options: By body odour and sensory organs detecting temperature and air current changes
By detecting carbon dioxide exclusively, with no other senses
questions.expl: Ticks detect hosts by body odour and possess unique sensory organs that can detect changes in temperature and air currents.

questions.q: What is the characteristic overall body shape of hard-bodied ticks?
options: Long and cylindrical like a worm
questions.expl: Hard-bodied ticks are shaped like a tear drop.

questions.q: The anterior gnathosoma (capitulum) of a hard tick bears which structures?
options: Epistome, hypostome, chelicerae, and paired palps
questions.expl: The gnathosoma/capitulum projects forward and bears the epistome, hypostome, chelicerae, and paired palps (4).

questions.q: The leg-bearing region of the idiosoma in a hard tick is called the:
questions.expl: The idiosoma has a leg-bearing region called the podosoma.

questions.q: The scutum of a hard tick is:
options: A soft membranous patch found only in females
The hard chitinous dorsal shield, notably large in males
A structure unique to soft ticks
questions.expl: The scutum is the hard chitinous dorsal shield of hard ticks, and it is large in males.

questions.q: Which structures form the excretory organs of hard ticks?
questions.expl: Malpighian tubules form the excretory organs in hard ticks.

questions.q: How many larval and nymphal instars does a typical hard tick have?
options: One larval instar (hexapod) and one nymphal instar (octopod)
Three larval instars and five nymphal instars
No larval instar, only nymphal instars
Two larval instars and two nymphal instars
questions.expl: Hard ticks have one larval instar (hexapod, six-legged) and one nymphal instar (octopod, eight-legged).

questions.q: How does adult feeding behaviour differ between male and female hard ticks?
options: Both sexes feed identically for a few minutes
Females take large blood volumes and feed for up to four weeks; males take smaller meals and attach briefly
Males feed for weeks while females barely feed at all
Neither sex feeds as an adult
questions.expl: Adult female hard ticks take large volumes of blood and feed for up to four weeks, while males take smaller blood meals and remain attached for a short time.

questions.q: Approximately how many eggs can a female hard tick lay, and in what form?
options: 1,000 to 20,000 eggs, in a gelatinous mass
Exactly 100 eggs, laid in a hard shell
Millions of eggs, laid in water
questions.expl: Female hard ticks lay large numbers of eggs — 1,000 to 20,000 — in a gelatinous mass, with egg laying lasting up to 5 weeks.

questions.q: Which genus is a classic example of a one-host tick?
questions.expl: Boophilus is an example of a one-host tick, completing its entire feeding development on a single host animal.

questions.q: Dermacentor and Rhipicephalus are classic examples of which host-use strategy?
questions.expl: Dermacentor and Rhipicephalus are examples of three-host ticks, where the larva, nymph, and adult each feed on a separate host.

questions.q: Lyme disease, the most common vector-borne disease in North America and Europe, is caused by which organism?
questions.expl: Lyme disease is caused by Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato and represents the most common vector-borne disease in North America and Europe.

questions.q: Tick-borne encephalitis (TBE) is caused by a flavivirus and transmitted primarily by which ticks?
questions.expl: TBE is caused by a flavivirus and transmitted primarily by Ixodes ricinus and Ixodes persulcatus.

questions.q: Babesiosis, transmitted by hard ticks, is caused by organisms of which type?
options: Intraerythrocytic protozoa of the genus Babesia
questions.expl: Babesiosis is caused by intraerythrocytic protozoa of the genus Babesia (primarily B. microti in North America and B. divergens in Europe).

questions.q: Which of the following is classified as an arbovirus transmitted by hard ticks in the source material?
questions.expl: Colorado tick fever, along with Russian spring-summer encephalitis and Omsk hemorrhagic fever, is listed as an arbovirus transmitted by hard ticks.

questions.q: Tick paralysis is best described as:
options: An acute ascending paralysis, often fatal, caused by neurotoxins in tick saliva
A chronic joint disease unrelated to tick bites
questions.expl: Tick paralysis is an acute ascending paralysis, often fatal, caused by neurotoxins secreted in tick saliva.

questions.q: Which of the following factors contributes to the high vector potency of ticks?
options: Rapid, painful feeding that alerts hosts immediately
Persistent, slow feeding; high sclerotization; few natural enemies; longevity; high reproductive potential
Extremely short lifespan of a few days
Complete inability to be carried between locations
questions.expl: High vector potency in ticks results from persistent, slow blood feeding, high sclerotization, few natural enemies, longevity, and high reproductive potential.

questions.q: Which of the following is a recommended method of manually removing an attached hard tick?
options: Squeezing the body firmly with bare fingers only
Using forceps, applying a hot object, chloroform, or coating with oil, paraffin, nail polish, or Vaseline
Cutting the tick in half with scissors
Ignoring it, since removal is never recommended
questions.expl: Recommended removal methods include forceps, applying a hot object, chloroform, or coating the tick with oil, paraffin, nail polish, or Vaseline.

questions.q: Which class of chemicals is used as an insecticide against hard ticks?
questions.expl: Insecticides such as organophosphates and pyrethroids are used in hard tick control.

questions.q: Community-level tick protection programmes typically include which set of activities?
options: Surveillance, vegetation management, host management, targeted chemical control, cultural practices, and personal protection
Only spraying insecticide once per year
Banning all outdoor activity in endemic areas
questions.expl: Large-scale community protection against ticks includes surveillance, vegetation management, host management, targeted chemical control, cultural practices, and personal protection.

questions.q: Soft ticks belong to which taxonomic family?
questions.expl: Soft ticks belong to the family Argasidae, distinct from the hard tick family Ixodidae.

questions.q: Which soft tick species is known as the African relapsing fever tick, found only in Africa?
questions.expl: Ornithodoros moubata is the African relapsing fever tick, found only in Africa.

questions.q: What is a defining external feature that distinguishes soft ticks from hard ticks?
options: Soft ticks have a large dorsal scutum, just like hard ticks
Soft ticks lack a scutum and have a ventral, not dorsally visible, capitulum
Soft ticks have six pairs of legs instead of four
Soft ticks are always larger than hard ticks
questions.expl: Soft ticks lack a scutum (dorsal shield) and have a ventral, subterminal capitulum that is not visible from above — unlike hard ticks.

questions.q: In soft ticks, what is "Gene’s organ" responsible for?
options: Secreting waxy, waterproof liquid that coats the eggs
questions.expl: Gene’s organ secretes waxy, waterproof liquids that coat the eggs of soft ticks.

questions.q: How much blood, relative to their own body weight, can the soft tick midgut ingest?
options: Only a fraction of body weight
questions.expl: The soft tick midgut, with its numerous branching diverticula, can ingest blood up to 8 times its own body weight.

questions.q: Approximately how long can adult soft ticks live?
questions.expl: Soft ticks can live for many years — approximately 5 to 14 years.

questions.q: How many nymphal instars are typical for soft ticks, and what do they each require?
options: One instar, requiring no blood meal
4 to 8 instars, each requiring at least one blood meal
questions.expl: Soft ticks pass through 4 to 8 nymphal instars, each requiring at least one blood meal.

questions.q: Tick-borne relapsing fever transmitted by the Ornithodoros moubata complex is caused by which organism?
questions.expl: Tick-borne relapsing fever transmitted by the Ornithodoros moubata complex is caused by the spirochaete Borrelia duttoni, with rodents and other animals as reservoirs.

questions.q: Q-fever, associated with soft ticks, is caused by which type of organism and how may it also be acquired?
options: A rickettsia; also acquired by consuming contaminated milk and food from livestock
A virus; only acquired through mosquito bites
A fungus; only acquired via inhalation of spores
A protozoan; only acquired via water contamination
questions.expl: Q-fever is caused by a rickettsia and can also be transmitted by consuming contaminated milk and food from domestic livestock.

questions.q: Which statement correctly contrasts hard and soft tick capitula?
options: Hard tick capitulum is anterior and visible from above; soft tick capitulum is ventral and not visible from above
Both hard and soft ticks have identical, dorsally visible capitula
Hard ticks lack a capitulum entirely
Soft ticks have an anterior, dorsally visible capitulum unlike hard ticks
questions.expl: In hard ticks the capitulum is anterior and visible from above, while in soft ticks it is ventral and not visible from above.

questions.q: How does adult feeding time compare between hard and soft ticks?
options: Hard ticks feed for several days; soft ticks feed for about 30–60 minutes
Both feed for exactly the same duration
Hard ticks feed for 30–60 minutes; soft ticks feed for several days
Neither hard nor soft ticks feed as adults
questions.expl: Hard tick adults feed for several days, while soft tick adults feed rapidly, typically for only 30–60 minutes.

questions.q: Cockroaches belong to which order?
questions.expl: Cockroaches are classified in the order Dictyoptera, within the suborder Blattaria.

questions.q: Which suborder do cockroaches belong to?
questions.expl: The suborder is Blattaria — the source of the common name via the Latin blatta.

questions.q: Roughly how many cockroach species are known?
questions.expl: About 4,000 species are known, though only a small fraction live alongside humans.

questions.q: How many of these species are considered domestic pests?
questions.expl: Only around 50 species are recognised as domestic pests.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a common alternative name for a cockroach?
questions.expl: Cockroaches are commonly called roaches or steambugs; "waterbug beetle" isn't the term used in the source material.

questions.q: The word "cockroach" (Blatta) derives from which language?
questions.expl: The name derives from the Latin word blatta, meaning "cockroach".

questions.q: How do cockroaches typically relate to disease, compared with mosquitoes or fleas?
options: They transmit disease directly through bites
They are not associated with disease at all
They are not linked to disease by direct transmission, but can carry pathogens
They only spread disease through their eggs
questions.expl: Unlike mosquitoes and fleas, cockroaches are not disease vectors by direct transmission; instead they harbour and deposit pathogens as they move across surfaces.

questions.q: What type of illness are the pathogens cockroaches carry typically associated with?
questions.expl: The pathogens cockroaches carry are typically those causing gastroenteritis, deposited indiscriminately on food and equipment.

questions.q: What is the scientific name of the American cockroach?
questions.expl: The American cockroach is Periplaneta americana.

questions.q: Approximately how long is the American cockroach?
questions.expl: The American cockroach grows to about 30 mm (1.2 in) long — the largest of the three species covered.

questions.q: What is the scientific name of the German cockroach?
questions.expl: The German cockroach is Blattella germanica.

questions.q: Approximately how long is the German cockroach?
questions.expl: The German cockroach is around 15 mm (½ in) — the smallest of the three.

questions.q: What is the scientific name of the Oriental cockroach?
questions.expl: The Oriental cockroach is Blatta orientalis.

questions.q: Approximately how long is the Oriental cockroach?
questions.expl: The Oriental cockroach measures roughly 25 mm (1 in).

questions.q: How would you best describe the general shape of a cockroach's body?
questions.expl: The body is dorsoventrally flattened, ideal for squeezing into narrow crevices.

questions.q: What best describes the cockroach integument (body surface)?
questions.expl: The integument is smooth, shiny and tough.

questions.q: Why might a cockroach's head appear to be missing when viewed from above?
options: It is hidden by the large, rounded pronotum
It is smaller in nymphs only
questions.expl: The head is small dorsally and can be entirely hidden by the large, rounded pronotum.

questions.q: What structures arise from the last abdominal segment in both sexes?
questions.expl: A pair of prominent, segmented, pilose cerci arise from the last abdominal segment in both sexes.

questions.q: What type of antennae do cockroaches have?
questions.expl: Cockroaches have long, prominent filiform (thread-like) antennae between the eyes.

questions.q: Why can't cockroaches suck blood?
options: Their mouthparts have no piercing stylets
questions.expl: Cockroach mouthparts are built for chewing, gnawing and scraping and lack piercing stylets, so they cannot suck blood.

questions.q: How many pairs of wings do cockroaches typically have?
questions.expl: Cockroaches have two pairs of wings; in most species the female's are shorter than the male's.

questions.q: What are the thickened, leathery fore wings of a cockroach called?
questions.expl: The fore wings are called tegmina — protective covers for the hind wings, not used for flight.

questions.q: What is the primary function of the tegmina?
options: Protective covers for the hind wings
questions.expl: Tegmina act as protective covers for the membranous hind wings, closing like scissors.

questions.q: What best describes the hind wings, and their typical use in temperate climates?
options: Membranous; capable of flight but rarely used in temperate climates
questions.expl: Hind wings are membranous and can be used for flight, but roaches rarely fly in temperate climates.

questions.q: Where do cockroaches typically hide during the day?
questions.expl: Favouring warmth, they hide by day behind radiators and hot-water pipes.

questions.q: Cockroaches are best described in terms of activity pattern as:
questions.expl: They are nocturnal and rarely seen by day unless disturbed.

questions.q: For roughly how long can cockroaches survive without water?
questions.expl: Cockroaches can live without water for about 5–10 weeks, and many months without food.

questions.q: What is the brown, bean-shaped case that encases cockroach eggs called?
questions.expl: Eggs are encased in a brown, bean-shaped capsule called an ootheca.

questions.q: What type of life cycle do cockroaches have?
options: Ametabolous, with no change in form
questions.expl: Cockroaches undergo hemimetabolous (incomplete) metamorphosis — there is no pupal stage.

questions.q: How many nymphal instars does a cockroach usually pass through, and how many can Periplaneta americana reach?
options: 3 usually, up to 6 in P. americana
6 usually, up to 13 in P. americana
10 usually, up to 20 in P. americana
1 usually, up to 3 in P. americana
questions.expl: There are usually 6 nymphal instars, though P. americana can pass through as many as 13.

questions.q: Which virus is listed among the pathogens cockroaches can carry?
questions.expl: The poliomyelitis virus is listed among pathogenic viruses cockroaches can carry.

questions.q: Which of the following is a protozoan pathogen associated with cockroaches?
questions.expl: Entamoeba histolytica is one of the protozoa listed, alongside Giardia and Balantidium coli.

questions.q: Which nematode is associated with cockroach contamination?
questions.expl: Ascaris lumbricoides is listed, along with Enterobius vermicularis and Trichuris trichiura.

questions.q: Cockroaches are known to be the intermediate host of which organism?
questions.expl: Cockroaches serve as intermediate hosts of the acanthocephalid Moniliformis moniliformis.

questions.q: Which bacterium is listed as being associated with cockroaches?
questions.expl: Staphylococcus aureus and Klebsiella pneumoniae are the bacteria listed.

questions.q: Which fungal genus is listed as a cockroach-associated pathogen?
questions.expl: Aspergillus species are listed as fungal pathogens associated with cockroaches.

questions.q: Besides pathogen transmission, what other medical concern is directly linked to cockroaches themselves?
options: Allergy to the insect or its dried fecal pellets
questions.expl: Direct allergy to cockroaches or their dried fecal pellets is itself a recognised health concern.

questions.q: Which residual insecticide concentration is specifically mentioned for wall lacquers/varnishes?
questions.expl: Lacquers and varnishes containing residual insecticide such as 1% cypermethrin can be painted onto walls.

questions.q: Which of the following is a non-chemical cockroach control method?
options: Introducing natural predators like domestic birds
questions.expl: Non-chemical methods include biological control using natural predators like domestic birds, plus gel baits, adhesive plates and sticky traps.

questions.q: Which pair below are both examples of chemical control methods?
options: Insecticidal spraying and dusting selected sites
questions.expl: Insecticidal spraying and dusting selected sites are chemical methods, alongside residual lacquers/varnishes.
